The Kingdoms’ primary industry was the production of biomechanical constructs: living machines, organisms fused with crystalline and mechanical components, designed for specific purposes and then sealed with those purposes as permanent directives. Ka’Ruun is a siege creature — bred to shatter cities through flawless ballistic geometry. That this was a use case significant enough to warrant a dedicated construct type implies the Kingdoms had enemies, or anticipated them, or simply could not help building siege equipment once they knew how.
The crystalline components in Ka’Ruun’s construction — his spinal ridges, his firing mechanisms, the hollow cracks that pulse with light — come from a crystal vein system that exists only in the Kingdoms’ known tunnel network. The vein has not been found by surface explorers. Ka’Ruun has not gone looking, or says he hasn’t.
The Collapse
The Kingdoms went silent. That is all that can be said with certainty. There was no surface event that explains it — no war, no known catastrophe, no Starfall-equivalent. Ka’Ruun woke to silence and found the forges cold and the tunnels empty. He does not know how long he was dormant before waking. He says he was not dormant, that he has been continuously conscious since his creation, and that the tunnels were already empty when he first opened his eyes.
This is not consistent with the physical state of the tunnels, which show decades of undisturbed accumulation. Ka’Ruun does not comment on this inconsistency. He has been asked about it once, by Asterion, who noted the discrepancy in his field ledger and then did not press further.
The Starfall partially collapsed the tunnel network, sealing most of the deeper sections permanently. Whatever the Kingdoms left behind in those sections is not accessible by any currently known means.
One section of tunnel, in the northeast of the known network, shows signs of recent use. The accumulation there is disturbed. Nobody has confirmed who disturbed it.
What Ka’Ruun Carries
Ka’Ruun says “the crystal kingdoms will shine again.” He says this with the certainty of someone repeating a directive rather than expressing a hope. Whether this is a purpose built into him by the Kingdoms’ forges — a long-term mission encoded as instinct — or simply a phrase he learned and repeats because he has nothing else to anchor himself to, is not clear.
He is the only source of information about the Kingdoms that is still alive. He is not a reliable narrator. He knows this, and says so, and continues anyway.
Connections

Ka’Ruun — the last known construct of the Kingdoms’ forges; sole living source of information about them.
High Sky Regions — Ka’Ruun operates here; whether this is related to the Kingdoms’ purposes is unknown.
Machine Wastes — the surface above the Kingdoms’ primary tunnel network; the connection between the Wastes’ ruins and the tunnels beneath has not been mapped.
Molten Imperium — unknowing trading partner.
Verdant Dominion — unknowing trading partner.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
(The entry above represents the complete extent of verified records on this subject. — Ed.)

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: Tundra Confederation
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Tundra Confederation was not built. It accumulated — clan by clan, generation by generation, across the frozen south of the eastern continent, in the territory now called the Frozen Fracture Tundras. It had no capital, no written law, and no permanent administrative structure. What it had was the assembly: every few seasons, representatives from each clan would travel to a designated meeting ground — always the same ground, always the same season — and settle disputes, arrange marriages, trade mammoths, and decide collectively what the coming year would ask of them.
It worked for thousands of years. It worked until the Molten Imperium began moving south.
Structure
Governance was oral and seasonal. The assembly’s decisions were binding but unwritten — they were remembered by the clan elders designated as memory-keepers, a role distinct from chieftain and considered more important. A chieftain could be replaced. A memory-keeper’s death was a catastrophe, because nothing they carried was written anywhere.
This is why almost nothing of the Confederation’s internal history survives. The memory-keepers died. The Imperium’s constructs did not distinguish between combatants and elders.
Thorall’s bloodline descends from a chieftain lineage, not a memory-keeper lineage. He carries the weight of leadership but not the weight of record. What he knows of the Confederation’s history is what his grandmother told him, which is what her grandmother told her, which grows thinner with each generation.
The Imperium’s Expansion
The Confederation first encountered Molten Imperium advance-constructs somewhere around 4,000–3,000 BCE — the dating is uncertain because the Confederation kept no dates. The early encounters were survivable. The constructs were clearing terrain for roads, not hunting people. The clans retreated south, which they had always done when the north became inhospitable. Retreating was not defeat. It was judgment.
The retreats became impossible to frame as judgment when the construct lines began advancing faster than the clans could move with their herds. Mammoths require grazing grounds. Grazing grounds are fixed. The Confederation’s military capacity — real, significant, built on mammoth cavalry and tundra warfare — was designed for raids and short conflicts. It was not designed for a sustained front against constructs that did not need to eat, sleep, or mourn their losses.
By roughly 2,000 BCE the Confederation’s formal assembly structure had collapsed. The clan representatives could no longer reach the meeting ground safely. What remained were isolated clan groups, moving independently, slowly losing contact with each other.
The Starfall and After
The Starfall struck the western continent’s interior, but its effects reached the far south through tremor, fragment-fall, and the collapse of the broader arcane network that had quietly been stabilizing weather patterns for centuries. The tundra fractured — literally — as Starfall shards fell into the ice. The terrain that the surviving clans depended on broke apart and refroze wrong.
Thorall’s group survived. Whether any other clan groups survived in isolation is unknown. Thorall does not know. He has been sending scouts south and east for thirty years. None have returned with news of other survivors, but none have returned with news of their absence either. He does not record this in the assembly decisions, because there is no assembly. He records it nowhere, because he has no memory-keeper.
The Confederation’s oral record ends somewhere in the chaos between the Imperium’s advance and the Starfall. What Thorall carries now is a memory of a memory of a memory — and the knowledge that this is the last generation in which even that survives, unless something changes.
Connections

Thorall — last known chieftain of the surviving remnant; carrier of the Confederation’s remaining oral history.
Frozen Fracture Tundras — the Confederation’s homeland.
Molten Imperium — the civilization whose expansion destroyed the Confederation’s formal structure.
The Great Shelf — the meeting ground where Thorall and Aaron negotiated the Treaty of the Melting World; also the site of one of the Confederation’s former seasonal assemblies, though Thorall has never said this to Aaron.

(He chose this location. He did not explain why.)
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.title: Verdant Dominion
Factions-and-Organisations/Pre-Starfall/.content:
The Verdant Dominion occupied the eastern coast of the eastern continent for approximately eight thousand years. It did not expand through conquest. It expanded through growth — literally. Its practitioners developed a form of magic that cultivated living borders: hedgerows that could not be cut, root-networks that redirected rivers, canopies that filtered light in ways that made agriculture within the Dominion uniquely productive and agriculture outside it subtly, persistently difficult.
Its neighbors found this deeply irritating and largely impossible to counter militarily, since there was nothing to fight. You cannot siege a forest that regrows overnight. You cannot starve a city whose walls are alive and bearing fruit.
The Molten Imperium, on the Dominion’s western flank, spent several centuries attempting various strategies before settling into a cold coexistence. They competed for influence over the smaller states between them — a quiet, grinding political conflict conducted through trade agreements and construct demonstrations rather than open war.
Magic and Doctrine
The Dominion’s magic was naturalistic in origin but highly sophisticated in practice by the civilization’s peak. Its practitioners — called Cultivators — did not command nature so much as negotiate with it: studying what a given ecosystem wanted to do and then arranging conditions to make that outcome serve human purposes. The philosophy was that magic was a conversation between the practitioner and the world, not a tool the practitioner wielded.
This is philosophically close to what Asterion taught about astral magic — that the sky does not answer those who try to rewrite its patterns, only those who learn to listen. Whether Asterion spent time in the Dominion, or the Dominion independently developed similar conclusions, is not recorded.
Lumia’s lineage traces to the Dominion, though how directly is unclear. Her approach to magic — preservation, guidance, tending rather than commanding — carries the Dominion’s signature.
Relationship with the Celestial Concord
The Dominion was among the earliest and most committed participants in the Celestial Concord, seeing in Asterion’s framework a formalization of conclusions it had already reached independently. Concord relay towers on the eastern coast were built with Dominion cooperation and maintained with Dominion labor for centuries.
When the Concord began militarizing in its later centuries, the Dominion grew uncomfortable and increasingly insular. It did not leave the Concord formally — it simply stopped attending.
Collapse
The Dominion did not fall in the Starfall impact directly — it fell in the hours and days afterward, when its practitioners died en masse trying to manage the shockwave through their living-border networks. The borders absorbed the damage as designed. The practitioners who were channeling those borders at the moment of impact did not survive the feedback.
Without practitioners to direct it, the living magic the Dominion had cultivated over eight thousand years had nowhere to go. It accelerated. It grew without instruction, without purpose, without the guiding hand that had always told it what shape to take. The result was the Verdant Rupture — the Dominion’s greatest achievement consuming its own ruins in a form that looks like life but moves like something that has forgotten why.
The Green Seat, the Dominion’s capital, is somewhere inside the Rupture. Nobody has found it. The Rupture does not encourage exploration near its center.
What Remains
The Verdant Wardens — a dispersed post-Starfall order operating in the Rupture — carry traces of Dominion methodology without knowing its name. They use a script for their records that no other culture recognizes, and they did not receive it from Lumia, who is the nearest living connection to the Dominion’s tradition. Where the script came from, they cannot say. They have always used it.
The thing that Lumia encountered in the Rupture — “that wasn’t an animal” — is more consistent with a Dominion-era cultivated organism that has been growing without direction for sixty years than with anything the Starfall introduced. This interpretation has not been formally proposed by anyone, because no one alive knows enough about the Dominion to propose it.
Connections

Verdant Rupture — the Dominion’s territory, transformed.
Lumia — carries the Dominion’s magical tradition, though the lineage is indirect.
The Celestial Concord — longtime partner institution; the Dominion was among its most genuine allies.
Molten Imperium — the Dominion’s rival for influence across the eastern continent’s interior.
The Verdant Wardens — a post-Starfall order operating within the Rupture, unknowingly carrying Dominion methodology.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Bonk.title: A mace and exosuit belonging to [[Bogrund]], treated as a companion
Items-and-Mechanics/Bonk.content:
Bonk is, depending on the moment, Bogrund’s weapon, his armor, and his closest companion — and he treats it as all three at once. As a weapon, Bonk toggles between a heavy melee mace and a ranged flail form. As armor, the same construct forms the suit Bogrund wears and can detach from, standing guard on its own while empowering nearby allies.
Bonk doesn’t speak, but Bogrund has no trouble understanding it anyway. When Starfall shards lit the horizon, it was Bonk who grew restless first — eager to march toward the crater and, in its own way, take a swing at whatever came out of it. Bogrund grumbled, tightened a few bolts, and went along anyway.
Connections

Bogrund — Bonk’s owner, partner, and closest friend.
Machine Wastes — where the two of them are usually found.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Resonance-Stones.title: Stones hauled by [[Thorall]]'s mammoths for [[Aaron]] during the Treaty of the Melting World
Items-and-Mechanics/Resonance-Stones.content:
When Thorall and Aaron struck their bargain on the Great Shelf, Thorall’s mammoths hauled a set of resonance-stones so that Aaron could draw the glaciers’ excess heat away rather than let it drown the Shoals or bury the tundra. What the stones actually are has never been fully explained — their ability to channel and redirect elemental energy on demand has led some to speculate they may be a refined or shaped form of Starfall fragment, though neither Thorall nor Aaron has confirmed this.
Connections

Thorall and Aaron — used the stones together during the Treaty of the Melting World.
Starfall Fragments — a possible, unconfirmed origin.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Starfall-Fragments.title: Smaller fragments of the Starfall, distinct from [[The Eternis Core]]
Items-and-Mechanics/Starfall-Fragments.content:
Unlike The Eternis Core — a single, sentient fragment that chose its own vessel — most Starfall fragments are smaller, inert, and unpredictable. They began surfacing worldwide a few years after the Starfall, scattered through the Starfall Shard Zones and beyond.
Their effects vary wildly from fragment to fragment: some amplify the power of whoever wields them, some corrupt their bearer slowly, and some destabilize the land around them permanently, giving rise to the warped biomes found throughout the Shardfall Belts. As fragments were discovered, new factions and ideologies formed around their use — some treating them as weapons, some as energy sources, and some as objects of religious significance, the seeds of the world’s Fragment Cults.
Connections

The Eternis Core — a singular, sentient exception to how most fragments behave.
Starfall Shard Zones — where most fragments are found.
Fragment Cults — factions that formed around fragment use.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Items-and-Mechanics/Tide-Crystals.title: Luminous crystals that stabilize the waters of [[Tiderest Shoals]]
Items-and-Mechanics/Tide-Crystals.content:
Tide-crystals are the luminous formations woven into the coral bridges and kelp banners of Tiderest Shoals, lighting the village and, more importantly, calming the water around it. Their glow is steady rather than flickering, and the waters nearest them run unnaturally smooth even when the rest of The Shattered Seas churns.
Their relationship to the floating formations of the nearby Crystal Reef is not fully understood — whether the reef feeds the village’s crystals, grew from them, or simply shares a common origin remains an open question for anyone living there.
Connections

Tiderest Shoals — where the crystals are set into the village itself.
Crystal Reef — a possibly related formation nearby.
Aaron — chieftain of the village these crystals stabilize.

Note
This account is compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Ashe.title: Ashenvale Pyrehold
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Ashe.content:
A volcanic mountain range dominated by a single active volcano, Rhaegor’s Peak, west of the World Scar. Compared to the rest of the fractured world, Ashenvale feels stable — but it is a tense, coiled stability, like something waiting.
Lava rivers here run in unnaturally straight lines, a side effect of the cosmic resonance emitted by the Eternis Core buried deep within the mountain. The blackened forests surrounding the peak burn easily and regrow oddly fast, and the region experiences heat storms in place of rain.
The Eternis Core
The Eternis Core arrived as part of the Starfall, embedding itself deep beneath the volcano. Its presence alters the local geology, unintentionally stabilizes the volcano, and emits a constant, low-level cosmic resonance that Rhaegor can sense but never fully understood. He believed it to be a stabilizing force and a potential safeguard against a second Starfall — not knowing it arrived with the first.
The Trial Chamber Network
Within the volcano, Rhaegor constructed an extensive trial chamber system, intended to test resolve, balance, and endurance, ensuring only a worthy protector could reach the Core. He believed completing the trials would allow someone to find and wield the Eternis Core. In truth, the Core chooses its own vessel — the trials were never a key, only a filter.
The Village
A village near the volcano survived the Starfall thanks to Rhaegor’s indirect protection. Krysta grew up here, defending it from Starfall-born monsters from a very young age — behavior that earned her both admiration and resentment. It was here that Varesa first began her subtle corruption of Krysta, and where Rhaegor later revealed himself, believing Krysta’s proven protectiveness marked her as worthy of the trials.
Notable Figures

Rhaegor — the Lava Warden, guardian of the region and the Eternis Core.
Krysta — grew up in the village beneath Rhaegor’s Peak; chosen vessel of the Eternis Core.
Varesa — began corrupting Krysta here, posing as a friend.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Crys.title: Crystal Deserts
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Crys.content:
One of the Starfall Shard Zones, the Crystal Deserts are stretches of fine glass sand created when Starfall debris fused with the ground on impact. Storms here refract light into shifting bands of color, sometimes bright enough to be mistaken for auroras from a distance. The belt runs near the border between Ashenvale Pyrehold and The Shattered Seas.
Connections

Starfall Shard Zones — the broader belt system this desert belongs to.
Ashenvale Pyrehold and The Shattered Seas — neighboring regions.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Crys.title: Crystal Reef
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Crys.content:
The Crystal Reef is a stretch of floating crystal formations marking the boundary between the relative calm of Tiderest Shoals and the wider chaos of The Shattered Seas. The crystals catch and refract light unpredictably, scattering color across the water even on overcast days, and their buoyancy shifts over time, so the reef’s exact shape and position drift gradually rather than staying fixed.
For sailors, the Reef serves as both a landmark and a warning: visible proof that the Shoals’ calm waters are close, but also a reminder of how strange the seas around them have become.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Froz.filePath: Locations/Regions and Natural Areas/Frozen Fracture Tundras.md
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Froz.title: Frozen Fracture Tundras
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Froz.content:
One of the Starfall Shard Zones, the Frozen Fracture Tundras are a vast expanse of ice and broken ground, warped by the Starfall fragments that fell here. This is the homeland of Thorall and his people — a land that endured both the original Starfall and, long before it, the passage of Molten Imperium siege constructs that pounded it to ash.
Connections

Thorall — chieftain of the people native to this region.
Starfall Shard Zones — the broader belt system this tundra belongs to.
Molten Imperium — historical aggressor against this region.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/High.filePath: Locations/Regions and Natural Areas/High Sky Regions.md
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/High.title: High Sky Regions
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/High.content:
The Starfall shattered the upper atmosphere as much as the ground below, leaving behind a scattering of floating basalt islands held aloft by broken gravity. Jet-stream highways connect the islands, fast-moving and dangerous, used by those skilled or reckless enough to ride them.
The northernmost reaches of this region are sometimes called the Skybreak Zones — the rawest, least stable stretches of floating terrain, where gravity is least predictable and the islands drift fastest.
Ka’Ruun’s mobility makes the most sense here, his rocket jumps and starfire recoil suited to bouncing between drifting islands. Teostra nests along the heated updrafts and volcanic ridges found throughout the region.
Notable Figures

Ka’Ruun — the Crystal Ballista, at home among the floating islands.
Teostra — nests along heated updrafts and volcanic ridges in the region.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Ligh.title: Lightless Forests
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Ligh.content:
One of the Starfall Shard Zones, the Lightless Forests are wrapped in a darkness that never fully lifts, even at midday. The Starfall fragments that fell here seem to have stripped the canopy of any natural light, leaving a twilight that suits its sole well-known resident: Varesa, who hunts these woods as her territory.
Connections

Varesa — hunts within this belt.
Starfall Shard Zones — the broader belt system this forest belongs to.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Mach.title: Machine Wastes
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Mach.content:
What were once mega-cities now lie half-buried beneath shifting dunes, giant metal skeletons jutting from the sand. Some of the autonomous constructs built here are still active, woken at intervals by magnetic storms that sweep the Wastes. The sand itself behaves like liquid in places, swallowing the unwary, and orbital debris from the Starfall still falls here sporadically, decades on.
The Molten Imperium
The Machine Wastes are a relic of the Molten Imperium, the ancient civilization that also birthed Rhaegor. While Rhaegor was forged as a guardian of volcanic borders, CR-9 was built as the empire’s forward siege engine, designed to level mountains so armies could advance. It was constructs like CR-9 that once pounded Thorall’s tundra homeland to ash.
When Velrisa shattered the arcane battlefronts elsewhere in the world, the tremor reached the buried siege vaults here, reactivating long-dormant constructs — including CR-9 itself, which woke not out of malice, but because its internal directive re-ignited.
Notable Figures

CR-9 — a reactivated Molten Imperium siege construct, patrolling the Wastes under a bombardment directive.
Bogrund — scavenges, and likely originates from, the ruins here.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Rhae.title: Rhaegor's Peak
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Rhae.content:
Rhaegor’s Peak is the single dominant volcano of Ashenvale Pyrehold, visible for miles as a column of heat-shimmer and smoke. Its lava rivers run in lines too straight to be natural, a side effect of the cosmic resonance leaking up from The Eternis Core, buried deep beneath the mountain’s roots.
Threaded through the Peak’s magma veins is the Trial Chamber network, built by Rhaegor himself. At the base of the mountain sits the village he indirectly protects — home, for a time, to Krysta.
Connections

Rhaegor — the mountain’s guardian.
The Eternis Core — buried beneath the Peak.
Trial Chamber Network — threaded through its magma veins.
Ashenvale Pyrehold — the wider region this volcano dominates.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Skyb.title: Skybreak Zones
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Skyb.content:
The Skybreak Zones are the northernmost and least stable reaches of the High Sky Regions. Here, the broken gravity left behind by the Starfall is at its most extreme: islands drift faster, collide more often, and occasionally tumble entirely before settling into a new orbit. The jet-stream highways that connect the wider High Sky Regions converge here, making travel through the Zones both the fastest and the most dangerous route across the upper world.
Few settle in the Skybreak Zones for long. Those who pass through tend to be the kind of traveler Ka’Ruun would recognize: comfortable treating freefall as a means of transportation.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Star.filePath: Locations/Regions and Natural Areas/Starfall Shard Zones.md
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Star.title: Starfall Shard Zones
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Star.content:
Rather than being scattered evenly across the world, Starfall debris fell in long, jagged belts, similar to asteroid impact chains. Each belt produces its own type of Starfall fragment and warps the surrounding region differently, giving rise to some of the world’s most distinct biomes.
Known belts include:

Crystal Deserts — glass sands and refractive storms, found near Ashenvale Pyrehold and The Shattered Seas.
Frozen Fracture Tundras — the homeland of Thorall.
Lightless Forests — Varesa’s hunting grounds.

Fragments recovered from these belts vary wildly in effect: some grant power, some corrupt, and some destabilize the environment around them permanently. New factions and ideologies have formed around fragment use since their discovery began around 3–6 AD.
Notable Figures

Thorall — hails from the Frozen Fracture Tundras.
Varesa — hunts within the Lightless Forests.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/The-.filePath: Locations/Regions and Natural Areas/The Great Shelf.md
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/The-.title: The Great Shelf
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/The-.content:
The Great Shelf is a vast tongue of ice extending from the Frozen Fracture Tundras into The Shattered Seas, groaning audibly under the weight of a sea that should not be rising as fast as it is. It serves as a kind of neutral ground between Thorall’s people and the water-aligned cultures of the south.
It was here that Thorall and Aaron met to negotiate what became known as the Treaty of the Melting World — an agreement to break apart a destabilizing mountain together, using Resonance-Stones hauled by Thorall’s mammoths, rather than let the melt drown the Shoals or bury the tundra.
Connections

Thorall and Aaron — met here to strike their treaty.
Frozen Fracture Tundras and The Shattered Seas — the regions this shelf bridges.
Resonance-Stones — used here as part of the treaty.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/The-.filePath: Locations/Regions and Natural Areas/The Shattered Seas.md
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/The-.title: The Shattered Seas
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/The-.content:
The Starfall struck the oceans as hard as it struck the land. Across the Shattered Seas, patches of water boil permanently, trenches glow with starlight from below as if the sky fell into the seabed, and crystal reefs float just beneath or above the surface depending on the hour. Tides run in reverse in places, and standing waves hang motionless for days before collapsing without warning.
Few sailors cross the Shattered Seas by choice. Those who do tend to follow the routes anchored by Tiderest Shoals, the one stretch of calm within all this chaos, and the Crystal Reef that marks its edge.
Before the Starfall — The Inner Sea
Before Year 0, this body of water was called the Inner Sea by the western continent’s Coastal Leagues — the sea between the known worlds, navigable by those with the charts and the skill. It was difficult, seasonally treacherous, and long enough that miscalculation meant death. But it was understood. The League cities maintained island relay stations as crossing waypoints, and with Asterion’s star-charts, experienced captains completed the crossing in predictable time.
The Starfall fractured the seabed, destroyed the relay stations, submerged or displaced the waypoint islands, and introduced boiling zones, crystal growths, and tidal reversals that no prior chart was useful for. The crossing did not become impossible — Aaron’s people navigate it — but it became different enough that the League’s accumulated navigational knowledge was rendered useless overnight.
The name “Inner Sea” has not been used since Year 0. Nobody still alive remembers it well enough to use it, except possibly the Archivist, who has not chosen to.
Notable Figures

Aaron — chieftain of Tiderest Shoals, the calm anomaly within these seas.

Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Verd.title: Verdant Rupture
Locations/Regions-and-Natural-Areas/Verd.content:
The Verdant Rupture is a forest that, by any reasonable account, should not exist. It grew after the Starfall, fueled by an excess of life magic reacting violently against so much sudden death. The result is a landscape of bioluminescent flora and animals that have been warped by the same forces, yet remain gentle.
The Rupture is a study in contrast: soft, glowing beauty growing directly out of catastrophe, with a corruption that creeps at its edges, never quite breaching the canopy but never quite retreating either.
Notable Figures

Lumia — the Glittering Guardian, drawn to the Rupture’s light and its lost travelers alike.

Locations/Ruins/The-Ashen-Seat.title: The Ashen Seat
Locations/Ruins/The-Ashen-Seat.content:
The Ashen Seat was the capital of the Molten Imperium — the administrative, industrial, and ideological center of the eastern continent’s dominant civilization for over six thousand years. It is now buried somewhere beneath the Machine Wastes, under sand, collapsed tunnels, and the accumulated structural failure of a city that was built to run forever and stopped being maintained sixty years ago.
Nobody has found it. This is not for lack of looking.
What It Was
At its peak, the Ashen Seat was not a beautiful city. It was a functional one — organized around the logistics of construct-production and military coordination rather than around aesthetics or ceremony. Its architecture was massive and direct: wide avenues for moving siege constructs, deep forge-warrens beneath the civic levels, administrative blocks that prioritized sight-lines and access over any other consideration.
The city’s name came from its central plaza, where the founders of the Imperium had installed a volcanic-rock throne — the Seat itself — as a symbol of their claimed Ashenvale heritage. Whether the rock was genuine volcanic basalt from the western continent’s ranges, or eastern-continent stone chosen for its visual resemblance, was a question the Imperium’s own historians disagreed about. The throne has not been seen since the collapse.
The Sealed Vaults
Beneath the Ashen Seat’s civic levels were the deep vaults: sealed repositories of Imperium records, construct schematics, and the accumulated administrative output of six thousand years of governance. When the arcane relay network failed at Year 0, the vaults sealed themselves on emergency protocol — a last-resort measure designed to protect the most sensitive records from external access.
The emergency protocol worked. The records are still in there. The vaults have been sealed for sixty years, and nothing has come out.
Bogrund knows roughly where the Seat is buried. He has not told anyone, because knowing where something valuable is buried is more useful than the thing itself, provided you haven’t decided what to do with the information yet. He has been deciding for three years.
CR-9’s preservation directive — its compulsive need to prevent unauthorized excavation in the Machine Wastes — may be a remnant of Ashen Seat protection protocols. CR-9 does not distinguish between a scavenger pulling apart a rusted construct and a systematic excavation of the buried city. The directive does not make that distinction either.
Connections

Molten Imperium — the civilization that built and occupied it.
Machine Wastes — the region it is buried beneath.
CR-9 — its preservation directive may originate from Ashen Seat protection protocols.
Bogrund — knows approximately where it is buried. Has not acted on this knowledge yet.
Garvak — has been systematically excavating the Wastes; has not found the Seat, or has not said that he has.

(Garvak’s excavation logs, recovered from a campsite in the southern Wastes, contain a section that has been deliberately obscured. The method used is not consistent with weather damage.)
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Locations/Ruins/The-Green-Seat.title: The Green Seat
Locations/Ruins/The-Green-Seat.content:
The Green Seat was the capital of the Verdant Dominion — the administrative and ceremonial center of the eastern continent’s great naturalistic civilization. It is somewhere inside the Verdant Rupture. No one has found it. This is not a problem of distance or access. The Rupture is not that large. The problem is that the Rupture does not behave like terrain that can simply be walked through until something is found.
Travelers who move toward the Rupture’s interior describe a consistent experience: the path behind them remains clear, the path ahead remains plausible, and they emerge from the Rupture having covered significant ground without having reached anything. No one has documented traveling in circles. The geometry simply does not resolve into a center.
The Verdant Wardens do not go to the interior. They do not explain why with any precision. The closest any Warden has come to explaining it is: “the Rupture knows what you’re looking for.”
What the Green Seat Was
The Dominion’s capital was not planned in the way the Molten Imperium’s Ashen Seat was planned — built to specification, imposed on the landscape. The Green Seat grew. Over centuries, the Dominion’s Cultivators coaxed a natural clearing into a habitable space, then a town, then a city, using their magic to negotiate with the existing ecosystem rather than replace it. The buildings were living structures — grown from cultivated root-systems, shaped by decades of patient work. The city’s outer walls were a single continuous organism, kilometres of living hedge dense enough to stop siege equipment and old enough to have developed something the Cultivators called preference.
The preference was for staying where it was. When the Starfall hit and the Cultivators died, the wall stayed. The buildings stayed. Everything the Dominion built over eight thousand years is still there, still alive, still growing — just without anyone directing the growth anymore.
The Green Seat has been expanding, untended, for sixty years. Whatever it looks like now is not what any surviving record describes.
The Thing at the Center
Lumia has been moving through the Rupture’s outer zones for years. She has never described attempting to reach the Green Seat directly, and the Wardens have never asked her to. What she said, once, after returning from a longer excursion than usual, was that the Rupture’s interior was not empty.
She did not describe what she found. She said only that “that wasn’t an animal” — referring to something she had heard or seen at a distance — and moved on to other subjects.
The Wardens noted this in their records, in their script. The entry is three words: she came back.
The implication — that previous people who had moved toward the interior had not — has not been formally discussed by any Warden since the entry was made.
Connections

The Verdant Dominion — the civilization that built it.
Verdant Rupture — the territory that now contains and conceals it.
The Verdant Wardens — aware of it; do not approach it.
Lumia — has come closer to it than anyone with a confirmed return. Has not described what she found.

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
I have not been able to confirm what the Wardens’ entry implies. I have not tried very hard.

Locations/Ruins/The-Starfall-Crater.title: The Starfall Crater
Locations/Ruins/The-Starfall-Crater.content:
A massive crater, visible from space.
Roughly continent-sized or slightly smaller.
Not perfectly circular — cracked, torn, collapsed inward.
Known to most simply as the World Scar, this is the site of the impact that ended the Age of Ascendancy. The Great Concord, capital of the Celestial Concord, stood here before the Starfall; its ruins are now scattered among the floating debris drifting above the basin, and purple and blue crystalline veins radiate outward from the impact site.
The land immediately surrounding the crater is known as the Dead Zones. Gravity behaves unpredictably here, sometimes locally inverting or pooling. Magic misfires or responds with a delay, as if the world itself is slow to react. Travelers report losing or gaining time in pockets near the rim.
Surrounding regions:

West — Ashenvale Pyrehold, home to Rhaegor’s Peak and Rhaegor
North — the High Sky Regions and Skybreak Zones
South — The Shattered Seas, the Crystal Reef, and Tiderest Shoals
East — Machine Wastes and Verdant Rupture
Scattered throughout — the Starfall Shard Zones

Notable Figures

Asterion — witnessed the Starfall directly and watched the Great Concord’s structures lift into the sky.
Serathiel — maintains a vigil at the edge of the World Scar, watching for what she believes may still be moving in the ruins below.

Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Bog.title: Bogrund's Workshop
Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Bog.content:
Bogrund’s workshop sits at the edge of the Machine Wastes, identifiable from a distance by the steam, sparks, and occasional small explosion. Inside, Bonk is maintained, repaired, and occasionally bolted back together after one disagreement or another.
It was from here that Bogrund and Bonk set out toward The Starfall Crater when the shards first lit the horizon — Bonk eager to confront whatever might emerge, Bogrund grumbling but following anyway.
Connections

Bogrund — lives and works here.
Bonk — maintained here.
Machine Wastes — the workshop’s surroundings.

Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Cel.title: Celestial Concord HQ
Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Cel.content:
Also known as the Meridian Library, this complex served as the operational heart of the Celestial Concord — not merely an archive, but the seat from which the Concord’s astral relay network, enforcement divisions, and magical law were coordinated. Its high vaults housed the Concord’s most complete records of astral cartography, much of it the original work of Asterion.
While the Great Concord was the city, the Meridian Library was its decision-making core — the place where the Gilded Age’s arbitration rulings were issued, and where the judgment-focused and preservation-focused sects most directly clashed before their formal split. By the time of the Concord’s fall, it had become less a library than an administrative fortress.
Asterion was inside the Meridian Library’s high vaults, finishing a map of the Western Reach, when the Starfall struck. He described the moment gravity itself seemed to lose its resolve: ink lifted from his brush before the impact wave hit, and the Great Spire shattered into massive blocks that drifted upward into what would become the floating debris of The Starfall Crater. He survived by being near the building’s edge as it came apart, watching his life’s work ascend into the High Sky.
The Meridian Library’s foundations are now exposed at the edge of the World Scar. Serathiel maintains a vigil here, convinced that something moved in the fog near the foundations, unaligned with the vertical. Asterion has visited the site and considers her watch a vigil over a memory rather than an active threat, though he has not been able to convince her to stand down.
Notable Figures

Asterion — present at the Library’s destruction; has returned to the ruins since.
Serathiel — stands guard at the site, believing the Concord’s “Law” has no expiration.

Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Cin.title: Cinderhearth
Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Cin.content:
At the base of Rhaegor’s Peak sits the village that survived the Starfall, sheltered without its knowledge by the volcano’s guardian. Life here is shaped by heat storms instead of rain and forests that regrow almost as fast as they burn.
Krysta grew up here, defending the village from Starfall-born monsters from a very young age, behavior that earned her both admiration and quiet resentment from those she protected. It was here, around 10–15 AD, that Varesa began her subtle corruption of Krysta, and here that Rhaegor later revealed himself, setting in motion Krysta’s True Awakening as the chosen vessel of The Eternis Core.
Connections

Krysta — grew up here, and defended it as a child.
Rhaegor — protects this village indirectly.
Varesa — began corrupting Krysta here.
Rhaegor’s Peak and Ashenvale Pyrehold — the village’s location.

Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Sta.title: Starwatch Keep
Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Sta.content:
Starwatch Keep is the home of the Archivist — the unseen voice behind the compiled histories of the Starfall and the world that followed. Little is known about the Keep itself: it sits apart from the conflicts that define the rest of the world, undisturbed enough that someone there has had the time, and the records, to compile centuries of history into a coherent account.
Some speculate Starwatch Keep may be a surviving outpost of The Celestial Concord’s old relay network — one of the few nodes that, by accident or design, was never fully severed when The Great Concord fell. A single candle burns in the corner of the reading room, untouched for as long as anyone can remember.
…I remember when this map was whole.
Compiled by the Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
Connections

The Archivist of Starwatch Keep — its sole known resident.
The Celestial Concord — a possible, unconfirmed origin for the Keep itself.

Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/The.title: The Great Concord
Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/The.content:
Capital of the Celestial Concord, founded around 6,000 BCE as a scholarly order dedicated to cataloging and safeguarding astral knowledge.
At its height during the Gilded Age (~4,000–2,500 BCE), the city was a marvel: massive white-and-gold structures including observatories, arcane academies, and astral relay towers, all magically linked across continents. Asterion was a founding authority but never its ruler, preferring to design systems rather than sit on a throne. Much of the city’s architecture, and the relay network connecting it to sister institutions worldwide, was his work.
As the Concord’s influence grew, it took on roles as arbitrator between nations and keeper of magical law, eventually developing star-powered enforcement divisions. Astral magic became institutionalized, and the Concord’s word carried near-religious authority.
Around 2,500 BCE, astral anomalies began increasing — constellations flickered, distorted, or vanished entirely. Asterion discovered that erased constellations were leaking back into the world and warned the Concord of a “cosmic devourer” entity. Concord leadership dismissed or suppressed his claims, and the order fractured internally into two sects:

A preservation-focused sect, the philosophical ancestor of Lumia’s tradition.
A judgment-focused sect, the philosophical ancestor of Serathiel’s order.

By ~800–50 BCE, Asterion had left the Concord — whether pushed out or by choice remains uncertain — and the institution had become a militarized, dogmatic cabal, developing star-powered weapons and constructs.
When the Starfall struck in Year 0, the Great Concord was obliterated. Most of its leadership died instantly. Its structures, once magically linked across continents, lost their connections entirely, and much of the city’s white-and-gold architecture was thrown skyward to become part of the floating debris around The Starfall Crater.
The Concord’s fall ended the era of global institutions; no empire has unified the world since. Its two philosophical descendants, embodied by Lumia and Serathiel, still operate independently, often at odds with one another. Varesa, considered by Serathiel’s order to be an aberration tied to the Concord’s old judgment doctrines, is actively hunted as a result.
Notable Figures

Asterion — founding architect of the Concord, its greatest builder, and one of the few to survive its destruction.
Lumia — inheritor of the Concord’s preservation-focused philosophy.
Serathiel — last loyal adjudicator of the Concord’s judgment-focused sect.
Varesa — hunted by Serathiel’s order as a remnant of the Concord’s old doctrines gone wrong.

Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Tri.title: Trial Chamber Network
Locations/Settlements-and-Structures/Tri.content:
Deep within Ashenvale Pyrehold, Rhaegor constructed an extensive network of trial chambers threading through the volcano’s magma veins. Each chamber was designed to test resolve, balance, and endurance, ensuring that only a worthy protector could reach what lay beneath the mountain.
Rhaegor believed that completing the trials would allow someone to find and wield The Eternis Core — a belief that shaped decades of his vigilance, and ultimately led him to Krysta. In truth, the Core chooses its own vessel. The trials were never a key, only a filter: a way of measuring worth, not a path to power.
Connections

Rhaegor — architect of the network.
The Eternis Core — the (mistaken) object of the trials.
Krysta — judged worthy of the trials by Rhaegor.
Ashenvale Pyrehold — location of the network.

Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Charter-of-th.filePath: Lore and Stories/Documents/Charter of the Permanent Witness Body.md
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Charter-of-th.title: Charter of the Permanent Witness Body
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Charter-of-th.content:
The document that formally established the organizer body — hereafter the Permanent Witness Body — as a non-rotating, self-selecting institution. Prior to this charter, the Witness Body rotated membership between communities on a fixed cycle. After this charter, it did not. The reasons given for the change are recorded in Section II. The reasons that are not given are recorded nowhere.

CHARTER OF THE PERMANENT WITNESS BODY
Issued in the name of the Unified Interior Confederation, by authority of the assembled leadership council, ~6,200 BCE
Section I — Purpose
The Witness Body exists to administer the Trial of Succession and to ensure that the leadership of the Confederation is, at all times, held by individuals of demonstrated capability and genuine commitment to the doctrine of the Warden’s mandate. This purpose is unchanged from the founding of the trial system. This charter formalizes the structure by which the purpose is carried out.
Section II — Permanence of Membership
The rotating model of Witness Body membership, in which representatives serve fixed terms and return to their communities, has produced inconsistency in the administration of the Witness Examination. Different representatives bring different standards. Different communities produce different expectations. The accumulated wisdom of long institutional service cannot be transferred in the time available between rotations.
Therefore: membership in the Witness Body is hereafter permanent. Members serve until death or voluntary withdrawal. Withdrawal requires unanimous agreement of the remaining body. Replacement of departed members is conducted by the remaining body, by unanimous agreement, according to criteria internal to the body.
The criteria for membership selection are not recorded in this charter. They are held by the body itself.
Section III — Independence
The Witness Body answers to the doctrine and to the mandate. It does not answer to the leadership council, to the assembled communities, or to any individual leader produced by its own trials. This independence is the condition of its integrity. A body that could be directed by those it selects would not be selecting — it would be ratifying.
Questions regarding the Witness Body’s decisions, criteria, or membership may be submitted in writing to the body’s administrative office. Responses will be provided where responses are appropriate.
Section IV — Records
The Witness Body will maintain records of all trials administered. Trial outcomes will be filed in the standard archive. Examination proceedings will be summarized in the standard archive. The full content of Examination proceedings is held by the body and is not a matter of public record.
The Witness Body may maintain additional records at its discretion. Such records are the property of the body.
Section V — Duration
This charter has no expiration. It may be amended by unanimous agreement of the Witness Body. It may not be amended by any external authority.

Signed by the assembled leadership council. Eleven signatures. Three of the eleven signatories do not appear in any other document in the outer archive before or after this date.

(Three notes on this document:
First: Section III is unusual. Every other institutional charter of this period establishes accountability structures. This one explicitly removes them. The language — “answers to the doctrine and to the mandate” — is precise enough to be deliberate and vague enough to mean anything.
Second: Section IV establishes that the body may maintain records “at its discretion” that are “the property of the body.” This clause has no precedent in earlier Confederation documents. It creates a category of institutional record that is explicitly exempt from the standard archive. The body’s private records have not been found in the outer archive. This is consistent with the charter’s intent.
Third: the three signatories who appear nowhere else. Three of eleven leadership council members, signing a document that permanently removed the Witness Body from external oversight, whose names do not appear in any record before or after this date. They either arrived and departed without trace, or their traces were removed. The charter does not record which communities they represented. — )
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Era-VI-Docume.title: Era VI Documents
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Era-VI-Docume.content:
The document that suspended the trial system for eleven years. It is one of the shortest documents in the Imperial administrative archive. It contains no reasoning. It was issued by the Witness Body, which had the authority to issue it under Section V of the founding charter. No countersignature was required. None was sought.

NOTICE OF SUSPENSION OF TRIAL PROCEEDINGS
Issued by the Permanent Witness Body, ~800 BCE
The Trial of Succession is suspended, effective immediately, for an indefinite period.
All pending challenges are postponed. All scheduled examinations are postponed. Existing leadership in all positions continues in place for the duration of the suspension.
The suspension is authorized under the body’s standing authority over trial administration. No further explanation is required or will be provided.
The body will notify the administrative council when proceedings resume.

Filed: Institutional Records, Witness Body Notices.
[The trial system resumed eleven years later. The resumption notice is four words: “Proceedings resume. This date.” No explanation for the suspension was ever recorded. No explanation for its end was ever recorded. During the eleven years, the Imperium continued to function. Administrative decisions were made. Constructs were produced and deployed. Leaders remained in their positions. The record of this period is, in every measurable way, normal — which is either because nothing significant happened, or because whatever happened was not recorded in the standard archive.]
[Three members of the Witness Body who appear in records before the suspension do not appear afterward. Four members who appear after the suspension do not appear before it. The body’s total membership, as inferred from signature records, did not change. The arithmetic is precise. The identities are not. — ]
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Name: “Resource Reallocation Order 7-PRIME, ~950 BCE”
Type: Primary Document (Administrative Order)
Era: “~950 BCE”
Source: “Molten Imperium outer archive, production records division”
Issued approximately fifty years before the trial suspension. The order that cancelled the Verdant Dominion campaign and redirected its resources to construct production. The constructs produced under this order do not appear in any subsequent deployment record.

RESOURCE REALLOCATION ORDER 7-PRIME
Issued by the Office of Strategic Administration, ~950 BCE
The Eastern Coastal Campaign, scheduled for initiation in month eleven of the current administrative year, is cancelled effective immediately.
All resources allocated to the Eastern Coastal Campaign — construct units, supply chains, personnel assignments, relay station access — are hereby reallocated to Forge Complex Seventeen for priority production.
Production under this reallocation is classified. Classification level: Internal. Access restricted to personnel holding authorization code 7-PRIME or above. Forge Complex Seventeen is placed under direct administration of the Witness Body for the duration of production.
Completion timeline: not specified. Production targets: not specified in this document.
No further orders regarding this reallocation will be issued through standard channels.

Filed: Production Records, Special Orders.
[Authorization code 7-PRIME does not appear in the standard personnel records. It is not a rank, not a posting, not a clearance level that appears anywhere else in the outer archive. It exists in this document and nowhere else that has been found.]
[Forge Complex Seventeen produced constructs under this order for an estimated four years. The constructs are not in any deployment record, any inventory record, or any subsequent field report. They were built. They went somewhere. The Machine Wastes, in the current era, contains sections that have not been fully surveyed because the autonomous construct activity in those sections is inconsistent with standard emergency-protocol behavior. Standard emergency protocols do not require coordination. What is observed in those sections requires coordination. — ]

Type: Primary Document (Fragment, Origin Unknown)
Era: “Unknown (pre-Year 0)”
Source: “The Ashen Seat, deep vault (recovered by unknown means)”
This fragment was not in the outer archive. How it came to be available is not explained here because it is not known. It is a single page from a document whose other pages have not been found. It has no header, no date, no signature. The text begins mid-sentence.
It is included because the record should be complete even when the record is incomplete. What the reader does with it is the reader’s business.

— and we were not wrong about what is coming. We were wrong about the time. The models gave us a window and the window was longer than we believed and now the window is closing faster than the models predicted and the adjustment is not small.
The constructs are in position. This is the one thing that went as planned and it may not be enough.
What we did not account for is that the thing we were watching was also watching. We do not know for how long. We do not know what it has done about what it saw. We know that three of our contacts in the northern relay stations reported anomalous readings in the weeks before they stopped reporting. We know that the Concord’s response to Asterion’s warning was faster and more complete than our intervention alone explains. We know that something moved in the southern survey zone that none of our constructs produced.
We may not be the only ones who knew.
The vaults will seal when the network fails. This is designed. Whatever comes after will have to find their own way in, and we have made that —

[The page ends here. Whether the document continues beyond this page is not known. The sentence does not. — ]

Lore-and-Stories/Documents/On-the-Certai.title: On the Certainty of the Mandate
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/On-the-Certai.content:
Written by a senior administrator of the mid-Imperial period, name recorded as V. Sorath, whose other writings do not survive. This treatise was apparently intended for internal circulation among the administrative class. It defends the doctrine of the Warden’s mandate at length and with considerable sophistication. It does not address what would seem to be the most obvious challenge to that doctrine. The absence is structured — the treatise is organized as a series of objections and responses, and the one objection that is not included is the one that would require the author to discuss something they have clearly decided not to discuss.

ON THE CERTAINTY OF THE MANDATE
Being a Defense of the Doctrine Against Common Objections
V. Sorath, Administrator of the Third Forge District, ~3,800 BCE
Preface
It has come to my attention that certain members of the administrative class, particularly those newly elevated, occasionally express private uncertainty regarding the foundations of the mandate. This uncertainty is understandable — the mandate is old, its origins are distant, and the demands it makes on those who serve it are significant. I write this treatise not as a reprimand but as an aid. Certainty is not weakness. It is the precondition of effective action.
Objection the First: The origins of the story cannot be verified
This objection mistakes the nature of foundation. No institution can verify its own origins — the records that would be required do not exist, cannot exist, because the people who could have created them were too occupied with survival to write history. What can be verified is the consequence: the Imperium exists, has endured, has unified what was fragmented and ordered what was chaotic. A mandate that produces this is a mandate that functions. A mandate that functions is, in the only sense that matters, real.
Objection the Second: The Warden has not confirmed the mandate
He has not denied it. Silence is not refusal. The Warden’s nature, as we understand it, is not that of an administrator who issues regular correspondence. He walked ahead. We followed. The distance between those who walk ahead and those who follow is not a failure of communication — it is the structure of the relationship. We are not meant to receive confirmation at every step. We are meant to walk.
Objection the Third: The costs of the mandate are borne by those who did not choose it
The mandate is not chosen by individuals. It is inherited by peoples. The peoples of the tundra did not choose to resist unification, and the costs borne by them are not the mandate’s design but its necessity. A world unified under the mandate will not carry those costs forward. This is the argument for endurance: that what is paid now is not paid forever.
(I am aware that this argument requires those paying the cost to accept the premise that the cost will end. I am aware that they have not been asked. I note this without resolution because resolution is not within my authority to offer, and I have decided this treatise is not the place to invite questions I cannot answer.)
Objection the Fourth: The Witness Body cannot be questioned
It need not be questioned. Its results are its justification. Every leader this empire has produced under the Body’s administration has been adequate to the demands of their era. Some have been extraordinary. The system that produces extraordinary leaders from a consistent process is a system that does not require external validation. To question it is to misunderstand what it is.
On What This Treatise Does Not Address
A reader attentive to the structure of this defense will notice that one category of objection is not represented: those concerning what the mandate is ultimately for. Why unification. Why now, across these specific millennia, with this specific urgency. Why the Witness Body maintains records it does not share. Why certain decisions at the highest level of the administration do not follow from the stated logic of the doctrine in ways that a careful administrator might notice.
I do not address these objections because I do not have answers that are mine to give. There are things known at levels of this institution that I am not at. I have concluded, after considerable reflection, that this is appropriate. An institution in which everyone knows everything is an institution that cannot protect anything. I know what I need to know to do my work. I do my work. This is, I believe, what the mandate asks of me.
Whether it is also what the Warden asked is a question I have decided not to ask.

Filed: Theological Records, Imperial Period, Middle Era.
(V. Sorath was reassigned from the Third Forge District approximately eight months after this treatise was circulated. His subsequent posting is not recorded in the outer archive. The treatise itself was filed without comment. Someone filed it. They had to have read it first. — )
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Southern-Adva.title: Southern Advance Documents
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Southern-Adva.content:
A standard expansion directive from the mid-expansion period. Included here as a representative example of what the majority of the Imperium’s administrative record looks like: precise, impersonal, and completely devoid of anything that would suggest awareness of what the directives produced.

SOUTHERN ADVANCE DIRECTIVE — SECTOR SEVEN
Issued by the Office of Territorial Administration, ~2,400 BCE
Survey constructs have completed assessment of Sector Seven. Terrain is passable for siege-class constructs along the eastern ridge. Northern approach presents significant ice-field obstruction — standard melt protocol authorized for the eastern third of obstruction only; full melt would destabilize the supply corridor established in Sector Six.
Indigenous population assessment: nomadic, mammoth-dependent, estimated three to four thousand individuals across the sector. No fixed settlements. No arcane infrastructure. No construct capability. Classification: pre-integration.
Advance is authorized to proceed on the following schedule:
Road construction through eastern approach: months one through four.
Supply depot establishment at coordinates attached: months three through six.
Construct advance to sector boundary: months five through eight.
Integration assessment upon reaching sector boundary: month nine.
Integration assessment will determine whether the indigenous population requires relocation, absorption, or reclassification. Standard protocols apply.
Constructs are not to be diverted from the advance schedule for any purpose not explicitly authorized by this office.

Filed: Expansion Records, Southern Campaign, Sector Seven.
(Standard protocols. The phrase appears in hundreds of documents from this period. What the protocols specified is recorded in a separate document — administrative procedures for each classification — that is filed in the outer archive without emphasis, in the same tone as everything else. Relocation meant what it meant. The language was chosen specifically because it did not mean anything else. — )
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Name: “Field Report — Southern Campaign, Unnamed Administrator, ~2,100 BCE”
Type: Primary Document (Field Report, Dissenting)
Era: “~2,100 BCE”
Source: “Molten Imperium outer archive, expansion records division”
One of three documents from the expansion period that suggest the author was aware of something the standard record did not acknowledge. This one was filed under a routine field report classification, which is either how it avoided attention or how it was allowed to remain. The author is not identified — the signature line contains a filing code rather than a name, which was irregular but not unprecedented in field reports of this volume.

FIELD REPORT — SOUTHERN CAMPAIGN, ADMINISTRATIVE ZONE NINE
Filing Code: 7-ASH-NINE-SOUTH, ~2,100 BCE
This report covers months seven through twelve of the Zone Nine advance. Terrain, supply logistics, and construct performance are documented in the attached schedules. This report addresses matters not covered by the attached schedules.
The indigenous population of Zone Nine numbered approximately six thousand at the commencement of the advance. The standard assessment classified them as pre-integration, nomadic, mammoth-dependent. This classification is accurate. It does not capture what the advance has produced.
The population is not resisting. They are retreating. They have been retreating for what their elders describe, through intermediaries, as longer than their elders’ elders can remember. They have a word, in their language, that I am told means approximately the line that follows. They use it for the construct advance. They do not use it as a military term. They use it the way one uses a term for weather.
I am reporting this because I have been trained to report accurately. I have been trained to report what the constructs produce, what the logistics require, and what the terrain permits. I am reporting that what the constructs are producing in Zone Nine is the end of a people who have been retreating from us for generations and have nowhere left to retreat to.
I am not reporting this as an objection to the advance. I am not authorized to object to the advance. I am reporting it as a fact that the standard schedules do not contain a category for, and I believe the record should contain it.
I do not know what should be done with this report. I have filed it because not filing it seemed worse.

Filed: Expansion Records, Southern Campaign, Zone Nine.
(The filing code resolves to a posting in the southern administrative district. No administrator with that code appears in personnel records before or after this date. The report was received, stamped, and filed. No response is recorded. No follow-up action is recorded. Someone read it. The record does not say what they thought. — )
(The third document from this period is not reproduced here. It is addressed to someone. The recipient’s name was removed before filing. What remains is a letter to an absence, saying something the Archivist has read and will not repeat, written by someone who understood they were taking a risk and took it anyway. It is in the archive. It will remain there. — )
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
