Lore-and-Stories/Documents/The-Molten-Vi.title: The Molten Vigil — Recovered Transmissions and Records
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/The-Molten-Vi.content:
What follows is a collection of transmissions, records, and fragments recovered from or relating to the Molten Imperium and its inner body, the Molten Vigil. They are arranged not chronologically but by what they illuminate — and what, placed beside each other, they suggest.
Not all of these documents were found in the same place. Not all of them were found by the same means. Some were in the outer archive of the Ashen Seat. Some were not.
The collection is incomplete. This is not an editorial choice.

I. Before the Doctrine
~8,000–7,500 BCE — Oral Fragment, Provenance Uncertain
From The Warden Walked Ahead:
In the beginning there was only the ground, and the ground was hot, and the heat was not suffering but instruction.
They had come from somewhere. Nobody remembered where. A being had come — not a man, not a god, something that moved the way fire moves — and the leaving had happened. In the version the archivist prefers, he said only: come, and did not look back.
They followed because something in the way he moved suggested they should.
The elders called him the Warden. The Warden of what was not specified.
— Reconstructed from oral tradition. Third-generation account. The two other known versions differ in ways that cannot be reconciled. Neither has been located.

~7,100 BCE — Trial Record, Witness Examination Notation
From Trial Record — Contested Succession:
Third Trial — Witness Examination
The challenger was examined by the Witness Body in closed session. Duration not recorded. Questions not recorded. The challenger emerged from examination and was confirmed as suitable to lead.
The challenger’s name was removed from this record before filing. This was not standard procedure. The removal was authorized by the Witness Body. No reason is given. The challenger led the Third Community for thirty-one years and was not subsequently challenged. His name does not appear in any other document in the outer archive.
(The marginal note above was added in early Imperial notation — at least two centuries after the document was created — by a hand that does not match any identified archivist. Someone knew the record had been altered. They wrote it down. They did not sign it.)

II. The Body Establishes Itself
~6,200 BCE — Charter of the Permanent Witness Body, Selected Clauses
From Charter of the Permanent Witness Body:

Section III: The Witness Body answers to the doctrine and to the mandate. It does not answer to the leadership council, to the assembled communities, or to any individual leader produced by its own trials.


Section IV: The Witness Body may maintain additional records at its discretion. Such records are the property of the body.


Section V: This charter has no expiration. It may be amended by unanimous agreement of the Witness Body. It may not be amended by any external authority.

Signed by eleven members of the assembled leadership council. Three of the eleven signatories do not appear in any other document in the outer archive before or after this date.
(A body that cannot be questioned, that owns its own records, that cannot be dissolved except by itself. The charter was signed. The leadership council accepted it. What the council understood they were signing is not recorded.)

III. The Empire at Work
~5,500 BCE — Forge Complex Nine, Monthly Production Ledger, Cycle 7
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, production records division. One of thousands of identical ledgers from this period. Included here because of the final line.

FORGE COMPLEX NINE — PRODUCTION LEDGER, CYCLE 7
Administered by the Office of Construct Output, Interior Ranges Division
Labor-Class Constructs Produced: 340 units
— Designation L-4 (excavation): 140 units
— Designation L-7 (transport): 120 units
— Designation L-9 (structural assembly): 80 units
All units passed standard activation protocol. Zero defects logged.
Survey-Class Constructs Produced: 47 units
— Designation S-2 (terrain mapping): 31 units
— Designation S-6 (arcane resonance detection): 16 units
All units calibrated to current relay network frequency. Zero defects logged.
Military-Class Constructs Produced: 12 units
— Designation M-3 (perimeter enforcement): 8 units
— Designation M-11 (siege support): 4 units
All units passed combat-readiness assessment. Zero defects logged.
Materials Consumed This Cycle:
Volcanic iron: enough to build approximately forty full-grown horses in solid metal. Arcane resin: 87 standard casks. Relay-grade copper: sufficient to wire a small city block. Binding compounds: 21 barrels. All within standard consumption parameters.
Personnel: 94 forge workers, 12 supervisors, 3 arcane calibration specialists. No personnel incidents this cycle.
Operational anomaly noted: Unit M-11-FOUR developed unsanctioned movement patterns during post-production assessment. Unit was disassembled. Components were reallocated to standard materials pool. No further anomaly.
Next cycle targets: As specified by the Office of Strategic Administration. Ledger submitted for standard review.

(Three hundred ninety-nine constructs produced in one cycle at one forge complex. There were, at this period, twenty-three active forge complexes in the Interior Ranges Division alone. The ledger for the following cycle begins: “Labor-Class Constructs Produced: 347 units. Zero defects logged.” The ledger for the cycle after that begins the same way. The machine did not stop. It did not slow. It did not ask what the constructs were for. Neither did the ledger.)
(M-11-FOUR developed unsanctioned movement patterns. The phrase is not defined anywhere in the outer archive’s procedural documents. It was disassembled. Its components were reallocated. The next line is the target for next cycle.)

~5,100 BCE — Witness Examination Summary, Candidate Designation: R. Vael
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, trial records division, Examination Summaries subsection. Examination summaries were filed in the standard archive per Section IV of the founding charter. They are summaries. The full proceedings are held by the body. What follows is the summary.

WITNESS EXAMINATION SUMMARY
Candidate Designation: R. Vael
Trial Cycle: Spring, ~5,100 BCE
Examining Body: Permanent Witness Body, full membership
Physical Trial Result: Pass. Candidate demonstrated exceptional endurance and combat proficiency. Ranked in the top seventh percentile of candidates assessed in the current administrative generation.
Strategic Trial Result: Pass with distinction. Candidate resolved all three logistical scenarios within required parameters. Scenario Three — the contested resource allocation under degraded relay conditions — was resolved using a method not previously observed in this trial cycle. The method has been noted for internal review.
Witness Examination Result: Pass.
Recommendation: Candidate R. Vael is approved for leadership appointment, Third Administrative District, effective immediately upon certification.
Appended Notes:
Candidate has resided at his current posting for four years. Prior to this posting, candidate served in relay station maintenance for eleven years. Candidate has no documented family connections to the existing administrative class.
Candidate demonstrated, during informal observation periods preceding the trial, an interest in astronomical phenomena inconsistent with his stated professional focus. This interest was not raised during the examination. It is noted here for the body’s records.
Candidate’s social contacts over the four-year observation period include three individuals of interest to the body’s ongoing assessment programs. Contact with all three was initiated by the candidate without apparent awareness of their status. The nature of the contacts was assessed as incidental.
Candidate is not aware he has been under observation. He is not to be informed.

(The summary ends there. R. Vael is appointed to the Third Administrative District. He does not appear in the outer archive again for six years, at which point he is referenced in a resource allocation document as having authorized a survey of the northern relay stations. The authorization is within his administrative remit. The survey was conducted. Its findings are not in the outer archive.)
(The method Candidate Vael used to resolve Scenario Three — noted for internal review — does not appear in any subsequent procedural document. What the internal review found is not in the outer archive. Whether R. Vael knew that the body found his method interesting enough to note is not established.)
(The body passed him. The body watched him. These are not contradictory actions.)

IV. What the Body Knew
The Molten Vigil’s private astronomical records have not been recovered. What follows is reconstructed from three indirect references in the outer archive — documents that cite conclusions only derivable from a sustained private study of the sky.
Reference One — administrative correspondence, ~5,800 BCE, author unknown:
“The body’s findings regarding the northern stellar drift are consistent with our own survey data and inconsistent with natural variation. The timeline implied is not one we can act on in the current generation. We can act on it across generations. This is what we are for.”
Reference Two — internal notation on a resource allocation document, ~4,900 BCE:
“Approved. The observatory expansion serves purposes the standard justification does not fully describe. The body is aware of this. The body considers it appropriate.”
Reference Three — marginal note on a Concord relay station maintenance report, ~4,200 BCE, in handwriting that does not match any known Concord administrator:
“Cross-referenced against internal models. Deviation within acceptable range. Monitoring continues.”
(Three documents across sixteen hundred years. The handwriting in the third does not belong to any identified Concord administrator. Someone was reading the Concord’s relay station reports and annotating them for their own records. The annotation is calm. Whatever they found was within acceptable range. The range itself is not defined anywhere in the outer archive.)

V. Administrative Actions
~3,200 BCE — Personnel Transfer Notice, V. Sorath
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, personnel records division. One page. Filed without cover documentation.

NOTICE OF PERSONNEL TRANSFER
Subject: V. Sorath, Administrator, Third Forge District
Issued by: Office of Administrative Oversight
V. Sorath is hereby transferred from his current posting effective the date of this notice.
New posting: [not specified]
Transfer duration: [not specified]
Reason for transfer: administrative reassignment
This transfer is authorized under standard personnel reallocation provisions.
Signed: Overseer-Designate T. Cavren, Office of Administrative Oversight

(V. Sorath wrote On the Certainty of the Mandate approximately eight months before this notice was issued. The treatise was circulated internally. It asked, carefully, a question about why the Witness Body maintains records it does not share. It did not press the question. It explicitly declined to press the question. It was filed without comment.)
(Overseer-Designate T. Cavren does not appear in the outer archive before this document. The title “Overseer-Designate” is not a standard administrative title in the Imperium’s personnel hierarchy. Standard transfer notices are issued by the Office of Personnel Administration. This one was not.)
(V. Sorath does not appear in the outer archive after this document. His new posting is blank. He had served the Third Forge District for nineteen years. He had never been transferred before.)
(The transfer was issued eight months after the treatise. The treatise asked a question. The question was not answered.)

~2,700 BCE — Observatory Maintenance Request, Interior Ranges Station Four
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, infrastructure records division. Filed under routine maintenance, which is the category it was submitted under.

MAINTENANCE REQUEST — INTERIOR RANGES OBSERVATORY STATION FOUR
Submitted by: Station Administrator K. Thren
Request Classification: Routine Infrastructure
Station Four requires the following materials for scheduled maintenance and operational upkeep:
Relay-grade copper sheeting: approximately 1,400 arm-lengths of rolled sheet, 3 finger-widths thick
Arcane resin, grade A: 34 standard casks (each cask sufficient to seal a door frame on all sides, three times over)
Precision lens assemblies: 17 ground-glass units, each the diameter of a spread hand
Structural binding compound: 9 barrels
Arcane-grade binding compound: 21 barrels
Iron framing, load-bearing: enough to frame a building of four large rooms, floor to ceiling
Stellar calibration instruments, Type 3: 6 units
Deep-sky observation apertures: 4 units
Estimated completion of maintenance: 14 months.
Personnel required: 8 specialists, 12 support staff.
Authorization requested from: Office of Infrastructure Administration.

Approved. — Office of Infrastructure Administration. Date of approval: same day as submission.

(Interior Ranges Observatory Station Four has a recorded floor area roughly equivalent to a large house — four rooms, two floors. The materials requested are sufficient to construct a building three to four times that size from the ground up, not to maintain one that already exists.)
(The request was approved the same day it was submitted. The outer archive contains 4,700 infrastructure requests from this period. The median approval time is eleven days. The fastest prior approval was four days.)
(Station Administrator K. Thren does not appear in any other infrastructure request in the outer archive before or after this one. Stellar calibration instruments and deep-sky observation apertures are not maintenance materials. They are construction materials for a new, significantly larger observation platform.)
(The maintenance was completed in fourteen months, per the follow-up filing. The follow-up filing does not describe what was built. It says only: “Maintenance complete. Station Four operational.” The station’s new capacity is not documented.)

~4,100 BCE — Field Personnel Record, Forge District Seven, Cycle 3 Workers
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, personnel records division. One of a very small number of personnel records concerning non-administrative, non-construct workers. The Imperium ran on construct labor. Human workers appear in the record primarily when they filled roles constructs could not — skilled craft, arcane calibration, interpretive judgment. This record covers fourteen of them.

PERSONNEL RECORD — FORGE DISTRICT SEVEN, CYCLE 3
Classification: Non-Construct Labor, Skilled Designation
Filed by: District Labor Coordinator, Office of Personnel Administration
The following individuals are registered as active skilled workers in Forge District Seven for the current cycle. Registration is renewed annually. Workers not renewing registration are considered separated from district service.
Arcane Calibration Specialists (3):
Maret, D. — 11 years district service. Specialization: relay frequency alignment. Notes: consistently high accuracy. No incidents.
Sorun, T. — 4 years district service. Specialization: construct activation sequencing. Notes: transferred from District Two following restructuring. Performance satisfactory.
Vel, K. — 2 years district service. Specialization: relay frequency alignment. Notes: apprentice designation, under supervision of Maret, D.
Forge Craft Workers (6):
Arren, P. — 23 years district service. Specialization: precision component finishing, M-class constructs. Notes: longest-serving non-construct worker in current district roster. Has trained four subsequent workers now in district service.
Bael, S. — 8 years district service. Specialization: precision component finishing, L-class constructs. Notes: no incidents.
Ceth, R. — 8 years district service. Specialization: lens and optical assembly. Notes: reassigned from observatory support role following Station Three decommissioning.
Forath, N. — 5 years district service. Specialization: precision component finishing, S-class constructs. Notes: no incidents.
Ilven, M. — 5 years district service. Specialization: structural binding, large-frame constructs. Notes: no incidents.
Thera, J. — 3 years district service. Specialization: lens and optical assembly. Notes: no incidents.
Structural and Physical Labor (5):
Dorn, H. — 16 years district service. Specialization: heavy frame installation. Notes: has requested transfer to District Nine twice. Both requests denied — district retention priority.
Kaen, F. — 9 years district service. Specialization: heavy frame installation. Notes: no incidents.
Orath, L. — 6 years district service. Specialization: material transport, oversized components. Notes: no incidents.
Peth, S. — 6 years district service. Specialization: material transport, oversized components. Notes: no incidents.
Renvar, C. — 1 year district service. Specialization: general physical labor, unspecified. Notes: new registration this cycle. Origin: transferred from civilian population intake, northern sector.

Filed: Personnel Records, Forge District Seven, Cycle 3. Standard annual renewal.

(Fourteen people. Twenty-three years of service at one end, one year at the other. Arren, P. has been finishing precision components for M-class constructs — the military designation — for twenty-three years. He has trained four of the people who came after him. His name appears in four previous cycle records. The record does not say anything about him beyond his specialization and his years. It does not need to.)
(Dorn, H. has requested transfer twice. Both denied — district retention priority. He has been installing heavy frames for sixteen years. The record notes his transfer requests the way it notes everything else: without comment. He is still there.)
(Ceth, R. was reassigned from observatory support following Station Three’s decommissioning. Station Three does not appear in the outer archive’s infrastructure records as having been decommissioned. It appears in earlier personnel records as active. It does not appear in later ones. Something happened to Station Three. The record of what does not exist in the outer archive.)
(Renvar, C. is listed as transferred from civilian population intake, northern sector. The northern sector in this period was the frontier of the Imperium’s expansion. Civilian population intake is the administrative category for people absorbed into Imperium labor pools from territories brought under control. Renvar, C. has been in the district for one year. The record notes no incidents.)

~3,600 BCE — Operational Closure Notice, Subject: Arven Doth, Trade Liaison
Complete document. Recovered from the outer archive, administrative correspondence division. Filed under contract termination.

NOTICE OF OPERATIONAL CLOSURE
Subject: Arven Doth, Trade Liaison, Concord Relations Office
Issued by: Office of Administrative Oversight
Classification: Internal
Following review of the subject’s recent correspondence and field activity, the Office of Administrative Oversight has determined that continued operational engagement with the subject is not in the Imperium’s interest.
Effective immediately, all active contracts, correspondence chains, and material arrangements involving the subject are to be closed. Personnel currently in contact with the subject through official channels are to cease contact without explanation and redirect any inquiries to the standard contract termination protocol.
The subject’s access to the Concord relations correspondence archive is revoked.
Our operative at the subject’s current location — the relay waystation at the northern Concord approach road, where the subject is lodged for the second night of his return journey — has been notified and is awaiting confirmation of this notice. The subject’s travel documents and personal correspondence are to be secured before the station resumes morning traffic. The subject will not require them.
This notice constitutes full authorization for all necessary actions to effect closure. No further documentation will be issued.
Signed: Overseer-Designate T. Cavren, Office of Administrative Oversight

(Arven Doth was a trade liaison working across the boundary between the Imperium and the Celestial Concord — one of very few individuals with legitimate reason to move freely between both institutions. The outer archive contains no record of what he found on his last journey, or what he reported, or to whom. The “recent correspondence and field activity” that prompted this notice is not described.)
(The operative at the waystation is not named. The notice was sent ahead of the subject’s arrival — it reached the station before he did. It knew his route. It knew which night he would stop there.)
(Arven Doth does not appear in the outer archive after this notice. His correspondence files were not removed — they were integrated smoothly into the existing record, attributed to a successor, as if he had simply been replaced in the ordinary course of administration. The integration was clean enough that it would only be visible to someone who already knew to look for it.)
(Overseer-Designate T. Cavren signed this notice. The same title appears on V. Sorath’s transfer notice two centuries later. Either it passed to a successor who kept the title, or it did not pass at all.)
(The morning traffic resumed on schedule.)

VI. The Mandate Defended
~3,800 BCE — Theological Treatise, Selected Passage
From On the Certainty of the Mandate:

A reader attentive to the structure of this defense will notice that one category of objection is not represented: those concerning what the mandate is ultimately for. Why unification. Why now, across these specific millennia, with this specific urgency. Why the Witness Body maintains records it does not share.


I do not address these objections because I do not have answers that are mine to give. There are things known at levels of this institution that I am not at.


Whether it is also what the Warden asked is a question I have decided not to ask.

V. Sorath was reassigned from the Third Forge District approximately eight months after this treatise was circulated. His subsequent posting is not recorded.

VII. The Advance
~2,400 BCE — Expansion Directive, Standard Form
From Southern Advance Documents:

Indigenous population assessment: nomadic, mammoth-dependent, estimated three to four thousand individuals across the sector. No fixed settlements. No arcane infrastructure. No construct capability. Classification: pre-integration.


Integration assessment will determine whether the indigenous population requires relocation, absorption, or reclassification. Standard protocols apply.

~2,100 BCE — Field Report, Dissenting
From Southern Advance Documents:

They have a word, in their language, that I am told means approximately the line that follows. They use it for the construct advance. They do not use it as a military term. They use it the way one uses a term for weather.


I am reporting that what the constructs are producing in Zone Nine is the end of a people who have been retreating from us for generations and have nowhere left to retreat to.


I do not know what should be done with this report. I have filed it because not filing it seemed worse.

Filing Code: 7-ASH-NINE-SOUTH. No administrator with that code appears in personnel records before or after this date.
(The third document from this period — the one addressed to someone whose name was removed — is not reproduced here. It will not be reproduced here. This is the only editorial decision in this collection that required more than a moment’s consideration.)

VIII. The Silence
~950 BCE — Resource Reallocation Order 7-PRIME
From Era VI Documents:

Production under this reallocation is classified. Classification level: Internal. Access restricted to personnel holding authorization code 7-PRIME or above. Forge Complex Seventeen is placed under direct administration of the Witness Body for the duration of production.


Completion timeline: not specified. Production targets: not specified in this document.


No further orders regarding this reallocation will be issued through standard channels.

Authorization code 7-PRIME does not appear in the standard personnel records. The constructs produced under this order do not appear in any deployment record. They were built. They went somewhere.

~800 BCE — Notice of Trial Suspension
From Era VI Documents:

The Trial of Succession is suspended, effective immediately, for an indefinite period.


The suspension is authorized under the body’s standing authority over trial administration. No further explanation is required or will be provided.

Four words when it resumed, eleven years later: “Proceedings resume. This date.”
Three members before. Four members after. Total membership unchanged. The arithmetic is precise. The identities are not.

IX. The End of the Record
Pre-Year 0 — Fragment, Deep Vault, Provenance Unestablished
From Era VI Documents:
The text begins mid-sentence. The page before it has not been found.

— and we were not wrong about what is coming. We were wrong about the time.


What we did not account for is that the thing we were watching was also watching. We do not know for how long.


We know that something moved in the southern survey zone that none of our constructs produced.


We may not be the only ones who knew.


The vaults will seal when the network fails. This is designed. Whatever comes after will have to find their own way in, and we have made that —

The sentence does not finish. Whether the document does is not known.

X. After
What follows is not a document. It is an observation.
The Machine Wastes, sixty years after Year 0, contains sections that have not been fully surveyed. The autonomous construct activity in those sections is inconsistent with standard emergency-protocol behavior. Standard emergency protocols do not require coordination. What is observed in those sections requires coordination.
Bogrund knows approximately where the Ashen Seat is buried. He has been deciding what to do about that for three years.
Garvak’s excavation logs contain a section that has been deliberately obscured. The method used is not consistent with weather damage.
CR-9 prevents unauthorized excavation in the Wastes with a consistency that exceeds any documented emergency directive.
These three facts are presented without connection. The reader may connect them or decline to.

One further note, appended separately from the rest of this collection:
The filing code on the dissenting field report — 7-ASH-NINE-SOUTH — shares its prefix with the classification code on the resource reallocation order: 7-PRIME. This may be coincidence. The Imperium used numerical prefixes extensively and inconsistently.
It may not be coincidence. If it is not, it suggests the dissenting administrator had access to — or was assigned to — something classified at the 7-level. Which would mean they were not simply a field administrator who noticed something wrong. It would mean they were someone the body had cleared for internal work, who then filed a report the body could not acknowledge without revealing that they knew who had filed it.
The body filed it anyway. The body did not respond. The body reassigned them to a posting that does not appear in the outer archive.
This note is the last entry in this collection because it is the most uncertain, and uncertainty belongs at the end.

This collection is incomplete. Several documents known to exist have not been included. Several documents that should exist have not been found. The gap between those two categories is not small.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
(I have been assembling this collection for longer than I will say. Some of what is here I found in the outer archive. Some of what is here I found elsewhere. The distinction matters less than what it means that I found it at all.)

Lore-and-Stories/Documents/The-Warden-Wa.filePath: Lore and Stories/Documents/The Warden Walked Ahead.md
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/The-Warden-Wa.title: The Warden Walked Ahead
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/The-Warden-Wa.content:
What follows is a reconstruction of an oral account, committed to writing approximately 4,500 BCE by an unnamed archivist of the early Imperium. The reconstruction is explicitly noted as third-generation — the archivist was working from a written account of a spoken account of a remembered account. The chain of transmission before that point is unknown. The archivist notes, at the end of the document, that two other versions of this account exist and that they differ in ways that cannot be reconciled. Neither of the other versions has been located.

In the beginning there was only the ground, and the ground was hot, and the heat was not suffering but instruction.
They had come from somewhere. Nobody remembered where. The elders said their elders had said their elders had said there was another place before this one, and that the leaving of it was not their choice. A being had come — not a man, not a god, something that moved the way fire moves, with purpose that needed no explanation — and the leaving had happened. Whether he spoke or whether he only walked ahead and expected them to follow was something the elders disagreed about. In some versions he said: this land will be yours and all lands after it, go and make them one. In other versions he said nothing. In the version the archivist prefers, he said only: come, and did not look back.
They followed because something in the way he moved suggested they should.
The new land was volcanic and difficult and theirs. The being of fire did not stay. He pointed — some said east, some said simply there — and then he was gone, and the ground where he had stood was warm for three days after.
The elders called him the Warden. The Warden of what was not specified. Some said of the volcano. Some said of the mandate. Some said of them, specifically, which the archivist finds unlikely but notes without judgment.
They did not look for him after. He had given them the land and the direction and the warmth of three days, and that was what he had come to give. What they did with it was theirs.

Filed under: Oral Histories, Pre-Imperial Period, Provenance Uncertain.
Note, ~4,500 BCE: I have written what I was given. I have not written what I believe. These are not always the same document.

(The gap between the archivist’s note and the document itself is exactly the gap between evidence and conviction that defines this period. Neither can be recovered. Both matter. — )
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Trial-Record-.filePath: Lore and Stories/Documents/Trial Record — Contested Succession.md
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Trial-Record-.title: Trial Record — Contested Succession
Lore-and-Stories/Documents/Trial-Record-.content:
One of the earliest surviving trial records. Written in a script that predates the standard Imperial notation by several centuries and required translation before archiving. The translation was performed by an unknown party — the translator’s name does not appear in the record. The original document is held in the outer archive. The translation is what is reproduced here.

RECORD OF CONTESTED SUCCESSION
Third Community, Interior Ranges
Witness Assembly: Eleven representatives, seven communities
The challenge was formally presented on the third day of the dry season. The challenger named himself before the assembly. The incumbent named himself before the assembly. Both were confirmed as eligible by the Witness Body.
First Trial — Endurance of Stone
Both candidates were required to hold position on the heated rock shelf for a period determined by the Witness Body. Duration not recorded. The incumbent withdrew at the point of incapacitation. The challenger remained. The challenger was confirmed as the victor of the First Trial.
Second Trial — Contest of Arms
Standard rules applied. Both candidates provided their own weapons. No substitutions permitted. The contest lasted until one party was unable to continue. The incumbent was unable to continue. The challenger was confirmed as the victor of the Second Trial.
Third Trial — Witness Examination
The challenger was examined by the Witness Body in closed session. Duration not recorded. Questions not recorded. The challenger emerged from examination and was confirmed as suitable to lead.
Outcome
The challenger is recognized as leader of the Third Community by unanimous witness assembly. The succession is binding. Any challenge to this outcome within the standard period requires a new trial before the same Witness Body.
Signed by witness representatives of all seven communities.

Filed: Trial Records, Pre-Imperial Confederation Period.

[In the margin of the original document, in handwriting that does not match the primary text and was not part of the original record, someone has written the following in early Imperial notation — meaning it was added at least two centuries after the document was created:]
The challenger’s name was removed from this record before filing. This was not standard procedure. The removal was authorized by the Witness Body. No reason is given. The challenger led the Third Community for thirty-one years and was not subsequently challenged. His name does not appear in any other document in the outer archive.
[The handwriting of this marginal note does not match any identified historian of the relevant period. It was added by someone who had access to the archive, knew the original record had been altered, and chose to note the alteration without explaining how they knew. No further context is available.]
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/History/The-History-of-.filePath: Lore and Stories/History/The History of the Unnamed World.md
Lore-and-Stories/History/The-History-of-.title: The History of the Unnamed World
Lore-and-Stories/History/The-History-of-.content:
Long before the Starfall shattered the world, civilizations rose beneath a sky that was already breaking. Power does not descend from gods in this world — it leaks through fractures in reality itself. Erased constellations. Unstable magic. Cosmic absences that answer when observed too closely. The Starfall marked Year 0 and collapsed empires, rewrote geography, and scattered fragments of impossible power across the land, leaving survivors to rebuild amid monsters, relics, and half-forgotten truths.
What follows is the long account.

Era I — The Age of First Civilizations (~12,000 – 9,000 BCE)
Mortal civilizations emerge independently across multiple continents. Magic exists but is localized, ritualistic, and poorly understood. Early astronomy develops for navigation, agriculture, and religion. Asterion is born human during this era — exceptionally long-lived due to unknown astral magic, and obsessive about the night sky from the beginning. He does not inherit a great world. He helps build the idea of one.
Era II — The Age of Constellations (~9,000 – 6,000 BCE)
Asterion pioneers astral cartography — identifying the stable star-patterns that influence magic, fate, and natural forces, and developing Constellation Lines & Star Points as a discipline for working with them. Nations rise around star-aligned philosophies. Early star-resonant artifacts are created. Asterion’s immortality becomes suspected, then confirmed — not through myth but through his own celestial modeling, which shows him as a fixed point across millennia.
Era III — The Founding of the Celestial Concord (~6,000 – 4,000 BCE)
The Celestial Concord is founded as a transnational scholarly order dedicated to cataloging and safeguarding astral knowledge. Asterion is a founding authority — not its ruler, never its ruler. Massive white-and-gold structures rise: observatories, arcane academies, astral relay towers, all magically linked across continents. Celestial Concord HQ — the Meridian Library — becomes the seat of power. The Great Concord is built as the capital city. The world’s most advanced institution takes shape, and Asterion designs much of its infrastructure while avoiding its throne.
Era IV — The Gilded Age of the Concord (~4,000 – 2,500 BCE)
Concord influence peaks. They act as arbitrators between nations, keepers of magical law, developing star-powered enforcement divisions and institutionalizing astral magic. With that power comes subtle corruption: knowledge hoarding, political manipulation, moral absolutism. The Concord does not become evil — it becomes certain. Certainty is the more dangerous condition.
Era V — The Age of Omens (~2,500 – 800 BCE)
Astral anomalies increase. Some constellations flicker, distort, or vanish entirely. Asterion discovers that erased constellations are leaking back into the world and warns the Concord of a cosmic devourer entity responsible. Concord leadership dismisses his claims. Internal fractures form around the question of what to do about a warning no one wants to hear — fractures that eventually become Lumia’s preservation-focused sect and Serathiel’s judgment-focused sect.
Era VI — The Fracture of the Concord (~800 – 50 BCE)
Asterion is pressured out or leaves voluntarily — even he is uncertain which. The Concord, without its greatest architect and most inconvenient voice, becomes a militarized cabal: dogmatic, politically dominant, developing star-powered weapons and constructs, and treating faith in the Concord as near-religious. Meanwhile, Asterion continues his research in secrecy. The Concord rewrites records. Compresses his legacy. Protects itself from his shadow.
Year 0 — The Starfall
A god-like cosmic entity — possibly The Cosmic Devourer, possibly something else — triggers the Starfall. Massive meteoric impacts devastate the world. The Celestial Concord is obliterated; most of its leadership dies instantly, and its magically linked structures lose their connections forever. The World Scar is born. Technology and knowledge regress by centuries. The Eternis Core falls with the Starfall, embedding deep beneath the volcanic region of Ashenvale Pyrehold. New monsters and altered species emerge from the wreckage.
Asterion survives — not because he planned it, but because he was no longer centralized.
Era VII — The Shattered World (~1 – 10 AD)
The world becomes scattered survivors: villages, nomadic clans, isolated enclaves. Former empires are lost or mythologized. Rhaegor survives within his volcano and protects the surrounding region indirectly — including Cinderhearth, a village near Rhaegor’s Peak, where a girl named Krysta is roughly twelve to fourteen years old. She spends the years immediately after the Starfall defending the village from Starfall-born creatures, earning admiration and resentment in equal measure.
Era VIII — The Age of Shards (~10 – 30 AD)
Starfall Fragments begin surfacing worldwide. Their effects vary wildly: empowerment, corruption, environmental destabilization. New factions and proto-nations arise around them — the seeds of the Fragment Cults that now contest the Starfall Shard Zones. Rhaegor constructs the Trial Chamber Network within his volcano, believing the trials are the key to reaching the Eternis Core. They are not. The Core chooses its own vessel: Krysta, who becomes its chosen bearer after Rhaegor reveals himself to her, roughly ten to fifteen years after the Starfall. She now carries three voices: her own, the Core’s (order, preservation, control), and a third that has been present longer than either of them realized — Varesa’s corruption, which began posing as friendship years earlier. No one knows the full picture: not Rhaegor, not the village, not Krysta herself, initially.
See: The Fractured Heart, The Will of the Survivor, The Whisper in the Ash
Era IX — The Age of Awakenings (~30 – 60 AD)
Champions emerge worldwide. CR-9 reactivates in the Machine Wastes when Velrisa’s unraveling sends shockwaves through the world’s remaining arcane infrastructure. Garvak awakens. Ka’Ruun discovers volatile Starfall power in the High Sky Regions. Asterion resurfaces quietly, tracking constellation echoes that have begun manifesting in the people he encounters — fragments of erased star-patterns that should no longer exist, each one a clue in an unfolding celestial mystery. Rumors of a second Starfall spread.
See: The Dragon’s Temper, Starfire Trajectory, Neutralization Protocol, Siegeborn Awakening
The Current Era — The Unfolding Storm (~60 AD onward)
The world is fractured but awakening. Nations form with conflicting goals: control Starfall power, prevent another cataclysm, exploit what the first one left behind. Asterion hunts The Cosmic Devourer’s traces. The Eternis Core’s will strengthens within Krysta. Serathiel keeps her vigil at the edge of the World Scar, watching for something she cannot name. Lumia wanders the Verdant Rupture, tending to the lost. Thorall and Aaron maintain their alliance across the melting world.
The Starfall is not finished.
See: The Hollow Vigil, The Current That Chose to Move, The Mammoth’s Burden

For all recorded accounts, see The Starfall Anthology.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
This account supersedes the version dated ~45 AD. Differences between editions have not been disclosed.

Lore-and-Stories/History/The-Starfall-An.title: The Starfall Anthology
Lore-and-Stories/History/The-Starfall-An.content:
These accounts have been gathered as received. Not all of what follows was given willingly.

The Overarching Record

The History of the Unnamed World — the long account. BCE through the present era.
When Paths Converge — the epilogue. Every path, one direction.


The Short Accounts
Filed by subject. Descriptions where available.

The Suit With an Attitude — Bogrund & Bonk — A workshop, a restless machine, and a direction neither of them chose.
Embers of Sanity — Velrisa — (no summary provided)
Beneath the Molten Throne — Rhaegor — The mountain speaks first. He answers second.
The Mammoth’s Burden — Thorall — A march toward a breach, and what the ground said before they arrived.
A Light for the Lost — Lumia — A traveler in the Verdant Rupture. Something in the trees that wasn’t an animal.
“The Arrow’s Shadow” — Varesa — (document unavailable)
The Dragon’s Temper — Teostra and Ka’Ruun — A ridge, a shard, and two different ideas about what “it worked” means.
Starfire Trajectory — Ka’Ruun — (see above; filed separately at subject’s insistence)
Siegeborn Awakening — Garvak — A reactivation. Purpose remembered. World above, unwarned.
Neutralization Protocol — CR-9 — A machine scanning the horizon. The horizon does not scan back. Probably.
The Fractured Heart — Krysta, Rhaegor, Varesa — Three forces. One chamber. No resolution yet.
The Current That Chose to Move — Aaron — The Shoals, a departure, and an old alliance recalled.
The First Light — Celestial Concord HQ — Serathiel at the ruins. Varesa in the shadow. An arrow nocked.
Condemned — Serathiel, Garvak — A war-cannon raised. A verdict disagreeing.
Ascension — Serathiel — A siege, a judgment, and the moment dawn became something else.
“The Weight of Seven Stars” — (withdrawn)
[untitled] — Xero & Rita — (not yet received)


The Long Accounts — Asterion
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony, 8,200 BCE — Year 0 — ~30 AD.

The First Anomaly — ~8,200 BCE. A funeral. A shivering star. The first suggestion that someone would need to outlive the sentence.
The City of the Unmoving Reflection — ~4,000 BCE. The Capital at its height. Asterion at the Great Fountain, touching water that had forgotten how to move.
The Edge of the Circle — ~1,500 BCE. The Council Chamber. The last time he addressed them directly.
The Day the Earth Lost its Weight — Year 0. The Meridian Library. Ink rising from a brush.
The Friction of Being — ~28 AD. A nomad camp. A fragment-seeker learning the difference between asking and demanding.
Beneath the Shifting Sky — ~25 AD. A ruined courtyard. An apprentice named Maren. The sea spray hovering in mid-air.
The Whisper in the Ash — ~30 AD. Ashenvale Pyrehold. Krysta training. Something Asterion misread.
The Will of the Survivor — ~30 AD. The Ashenvale slopes. What Varesa said while standing on rocks that appeared to be empty.
The Architecture of Preservation — ~22 AD. The Machine Wastes. Three parties, one site, no agreement.
The Treaty of the Melting World — ~25 AD. The Great Shelf. Thorall and Aaron, a mountain, and a question of whose catastrophe takes priority.
The Hollow Vigil — ~30 AD. The edge of the World Scar. Serathiel standing watch. Asterion sitting down and opening his ledger.


This catalogue supersedes the version dated ~45 AD. Differences between editions have not been disclosed.

Lore-and-Stories/History/When-Paths-Conv.title: When Paths Converge
Lore-and-Stories/History/When-Paths-Conv.content:
The crater grew brighter.
The tremors grew stronger.
And across the world…
A titan marched.
A machine rolled.
A boy flew.
A dragon snarled.
A sharpshooter nocked ghostly arrows.
A guardian glimmered in the dark.
A mammoth chief prepared his herd.
An enchantress burned.
A lava warden armed himself.
An engineer and his metal child marched to battle.
The Starfall called.
And everything powerful answered.

For the full account, see The History of the Unnamed World.
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Eleven-Year.title: The Eleven Years
Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Eleven-Year.content:
What follows is a reconstruction from several sources: personal correspondence recovered from the outer archive, internal Vigil records recovered separately, and two accounts from individuals who served under Kael Sorveth during his tenure as First Administrator of the Eastern Directorate. The accounts were given to different people at different times and agree on the events while disagreeing on what the events meant.
Kael Sorveth is the only leader in the Imperium’s recorded history who the Witness Body never formally assessed. The trial record for his selection cycle is missing from the outer archive. The body’s private files have not been recovered. Whether the gap is administrative accident or something else is not established.
— The Archivist

I. The Man Who Won
Kael Sorveth passed the trials at thirty-one, which was young — most candidates who reached the final examination were closer to forty, carrying the accumulated weight of two decades of administrative experience and strategic positioning. He carried eleven years of frontier posting and a reputation, among the people who had worked under him, for being difficult to lie to.
He was not magnetic in the way that leaders in the records tend to be described. He was attentive. He remembered things people had said months earlier and referenced them accurately, which unsettled people who were used to being managed rather than heard. He asked questions that had obvious answers and waited to see if you gave the obvious answer or the true one, and he remembered which you had given.
He passed the Physical Trial with competence rather than distinction. He passed the Strategic Trial with something the examining records describe, in the only surviving notation, as an approach not previously observed. The Witness Examination is not on record.
He was appointed First Administrator of the Eastern Directorate at thirty-two and spent the next several years doing his job with the same attentiveness he had brought to everything else — listening to the district reports, walking the supply routes himself, learning the names of the forge workers in each complex he visited. Not because it was good for morale, though it was. Because he was interested. He had always been interested in how things actually worked rather than how they were described as working, and the gap between those two things, in the Eastern Directorate, was considerable.
He did not, in those early years, think much about the Witness Body. It was an institution. It had administered the trials for longer than anyone could remember and produced the leadership the Imperium required. He had passed through it and come out the other side and that was, as far as he understood, the extent of their relationship.
He was wrong about this, but it took him years to understand how wrong.

II. The First Thing He Noticed
It was a small thing, and he almost missed it.
He was reviewing the previous administrator’s resource allocation records — standard practice for a new posting — and found a pattern in the forge complex assignments that didn’t follow the stated logic. Certain production runs were allocated to specific complexes for reasons the paperwork described as efficiency, but the efficiency calculation didn’t hold up when he worked through it himself. Complex Seventeen, specifically, appeared in the records more than its production capacity warranted, and in the years where it appeared most frequently, its output records were either absent or unusually brief.
He made a note. He did not file a report. He had learned, in eleven years on the frontier, that filing reports about things you didn’t yet understand was how you ended up in conversations you weren’t ready for.
Over the following months he found three more things that didn’t follow the stated logic. Each was small. Each was deniable. Together they suggested that some portion of the Directorate’s resources were being allocated to purposes that the standard administrative record didn’t describe, authorized by an office whose documentation he could find referenced but whose actual files he could not locate.
He mentioned this to his deputy administrator, Eryn Voss, over a working dinner. Not as a formal concern — as a puzzle. He framed it as an administrative inefficiency he was trying to trace. She was a careful woman, twelve years his senior, and she listened without expression and said she would look into it.
She came back to him three days later and said she hadn’t been able to find anything either, and changed the subject, and he noted the way she changed the subject — a fraction too smoothly, a fraction too quickly — and filed that away alongside everything else.
He didn’t push. He had time.

III. Varek
The Witness Body member who broke first was not who anyone would have predicted.
His name was Varek — a quiet man, slight, who had been on the inner body for twenty-two years and was known among his colleagues, to the extent that anything personal was known among them, for the precision of his thinking and the absence of anything resembling doubt. He had been the one, in three separate deliberations, to articulate the third position — the argument that risk must be assessed not by what a person has done but by what they might do, the logic that had closed Beth’s variable and a dozen others before her. He had made the argument calmly and been agreed with and moved on.
He encountered Sorveth at a district review in the second year of the administrator’s tenure. These reviews were standard — the body maintained observers at significant administrative postings, a practice so embedded in the institution’s structure that it had stopped requiring justification. Varek was not the observer; he was there in an official capacity, representing the body at the quarterly resource assessment. Sorveth was running the meeting.
What happened at the meeting was unremarkable. What happened afterward, when Sorveth detained him briefly on his way out to ask about a resource allocation discrepancy he had noticed — the same discrepancy, Varek realized with a cold feeling, that the body had been quietly managing for eighteen months — was less unremarkable.
Sorveth didn’t know who Varek was, not really. He knew him as a body representative, a proceduralist, a man who had come to observe the quarterly review and was now being asked about a number that didn’t add up. He asked the question the way he asked all questions: directly, without apparent suspicion, as if the answer were simply something he needed to know.
Varek gave the standard deflection. The administrator nodded, thanked him, and let him go.
On the journey back, Varek thought about the way Sorveth had nodded. It was the nod of a man who had been given a deflection and had noted that it was a deflection and had decided, for now, to accept it. The man knew something was there. He didn’t know what. He was patient.
Varek had sat in judgment on a dozen people over twenty-two years. He knew what it looked like when someone was going to become a problem, and he knew what the body did about problems, and for the first time in twenty-two years he sat with that knowledge and felt something that was not the body’s assessment of a risk variable.
He felt something closer to dread.

IV. The Argument
It took Sorveth four more years to accumulate enough that he was certain something was there, and another year after that to find a thread he could pull without alerting whoever was on the other end.
The thread was a man named Dorath, a forge supervisor at Complex Seventeen, who had been transferred out of the complex seven years earlier and was now running a small operation on the eastern frontier. Sorveth found him through the transfer records — one of many anomalies in the Complex Seventeen documentation — and visited him under the pretext of a routine frontier inspection.
Dorath was fifty-three and careful and had been careful for seven years, which is to say he had been living with something he had decided not to talk about for seven years and was very tired of it. Sorveth had a gift for finding people who were tired of their own silence, and he sat with Dorath for an evening and let the silence do most of the work, and by the end of it he had a partial picture of what Complex Seventeen had been producing and for whom and where it had gone.
It was not the full picture. It was enough.
He went home and sat with it for three days and then wrote a letter to Varek. Not to the Witness Body — to Varek specifically, at the address he had found through administrative records that the body hadn’t thought to obscure because nobody was supposed to be looking.
The letter was three paragraphs. The first described what he knew. The second described what he suspected. The third said: I am not writing to you because I think you will help me. I am writing to you because I think you are the kind of person who, when you sit alone with what I have just described, will find it difficult to continue as you have been continuing. I may be wrong. If I am wrong, I expect I will know about it shortly.
He sealed the letter and sent it and then waited, and while he waited he worked, and he told no one what he had sent or why.

V. Varek Alone
The letter arrived on a Tuesday. Varek read it twice, burned it, and did not sleep.
He had been in the body for twenty-two years. He had joined because he believed what the body believed — that something was coming, that the work mattered, that the cost of the work was not greater than the cost of inaction. He still believed this. He had read the astronomical records. He had seen the models. He understood, with the same precision he brought to everything, what the sky was showing them and how much time remained.
What he had not done, in twenty-two years, was sit alone with the body’s decisions and ask whether the decisions were what the original purpose required or what the institution had become comfortable requiring. These were not the same question. He had treated them as the same question. He had been very good at treating them as the same question.
He thought about Beth, though he didn’t know her name. He thought about the case — Depot-14-South-Logistics-F, which he had been present for, which he had articulated the third position for, which had been decided unanimously and closed. He thought about the reasoning and found he could not fault it. The reasoning was still correct. The variable could not be left open. He had meant every word.
He thought about what it meant that the reasoning was correct and that he could not sleep.
He did not write back to Sorveth. He went to the next body meeting and sat in his usual place and said nothing about the letter, and afterward he went home and sat with the question for another two weeks, and at the end of two weeks he had not resolved it but he had decided that sitting with an unresolved question was not the same as acting on it, and the body needed him, and the work was real, and he went back to the work.
He went back to the work for eight more months. Then something happened that he had not anticipated.
The body assessed Sorveth.

VI. The Assessment
The risk assessment for Sorveth was twelve pages, which was longer than any the body had produced. This was because Sorveth was not a depot administrator or a trade liaison. He was the First Administrator of the Eastern Directorate, selected by the body’s own trial system, and closing his variable required a level of care that closing Beth’s had not.
Varek read the twelve pages and felt the reasoning close around him like something he had built himself and could no longer leave.
The assessment was thorough. It documented Sorveth’s movements, his contacts, his correspondences. It documented the meeting with Dorath. It documented, with a specificity that meant the body had known about the letter before Varek had burned it, the letter Sorveth had sent. It noted that Varek had not disclosed the letter to the body, which the assessment described as a monitoring anomaly requiring separate review.
The assessment’s conclusion was the same conclusion it always was. The variable could not be left open.
Varek read the final page twice, and then he did something he had never done in twenty-two years of body membership. He asked for a deliberation.

VII. The Deliberation
He made the argument carefully. He had always been careful.
He said: Sorveth was selected by our own system. If our system produces men who notice what he noticed and ask what he asked, then closing his variable does not solve our problem. It confirms that the problem is us.
He said: we have been managing the world for three thousand years on the basis that we know what is coming and nobody else does. We have killed people who noticed the edges of what we do. We have bent institutions that were working toward the same end we are working toward. At some point the question is not whether we are right about the threat. The question is whether what we have become is capable of addressing it, or whether we have spent so long managing variables that we have forgotten what the variables are for.
He said: Sorveth does not know what we are. He knows something is there. If we close his variable, we lose a leader the system correctly identified as extraordinary, and we confirm to ourselves that we can do this indefinitely. If we bring him in — not to the body, not fully, but enough — we gain someone who has already proven he can see what we do not want seen, which is exactly the capacity we need.
The body listened. The body deliberated. The body’s response was patient and thorough and engaged with every point he made, and at the end of it the body’s position was unchanged, and the reasoning — which Varek could not fault, which he had helped build over twenty-two years — closed around the question the same way it always had.
The variable could not be left open.
Varek was asked, at the end of the deliberation, whether his own variable required assessment.
He said no. He said he understood the body’s position and would continue his work.
He went home. He sat for a long time. Then he wrote a letter to a man named Sela, who had been on the body for eleven years and whom Varek had recruited personally and who was, as far as Varek knew, the only other member who had ever shown anything resembling doubt in a closed session.
The letter was two sentences. They are going to close Sorveth. I think we both know what that means for the work.

VIII. Sela
Sela was younger than Varek by fifteen years and had joined the body for different reasons. She had not joined because of the astronomical data — she had joined because Varek had recruited her, and Varek had recruited her because she was brilliant and because her particular brilliance was the ability to hold two contradictory things simultaneously without resolving them prematurely, which was a capacity the body needed and rarely found.
She had been holding two contradictory things for eleven years. The body’s purpose, which she believed in, and the body’s methods, which she had been accommodating rather than believing in. She had told herself the accommodation was temporary — that she was new, that she would understand better when she had more context, that the cases that troubled her would trouble her less once she had the full picture. She had been waiting for the full picture for eleven years.
She read Varek’s letter and understood it was not about Sorveth. It was about whether she was still waiting.
She wrote back: What are you asking me to do?
He wrote back: Nothing yet. I am asking you to know.
She knew. She had known for a long time. She went to the next body meeting and said nothing, and she went to the meeting after that and said nothing, and she went home each time and sat with the two contradictory things and felt the weight of them differently now — less like a condition she was living with and more like a decision she was not yet making.

IX. Sorveth at the End
Sorveth was fifty-one when he understood what he had been dealing with.
He understood it not through a revelation but through an accumulation — a pattern that resolved, one evening in his study, from a collection of separate observations into a single coherent picture. The hidden allocations. The body’s unrecorded deliberations. The personnel transfers that had no administrative logic. The people who had asked too much and disappeared into postings that didn’t exist. He had been assembling the picture for years without seeing it whole, and then one evening he saw it whole.
He sat with it for a long time.
He was not afraid, exactly. He had been afraid before — on the frontier, in situations that had a logic to them, where the danger was external and the response was knowable. This was different. This was the understanding that the institution he had served for twenty years, that had selected him and trusted him with the Eastern Directorate, had been watching him for the entire duration of that service, had read his mail, had assessed his risk, and had — he understood this clearly — decided something about him that had not yet been carried out.
He thought about writing to Varek again. He decided against it. If Varek had received the first letter and not acted against him, something had shifted there, and pulling on that thread might resolve it in the wrong direction.
He thought about what he could do with what he knew, and concluded the answer was almost nothing. He had no proof of anything that would survive outside his own understanding. He had a pattern, a picture assembled from gaps and anomalies, and the people who would need to be convinced were the same people the body had been managing for centuries.
He wrote in his journal that evening — he had always kept a journal, openly, which in retrospect he understood was the reason he was still alive, because a man who writes openly is less dangerous than a man who hides things — and he wrote: I have been fighting something I couldn’t name for twenty years. I know its name now. I don’t think the name changes anything except how I feel about what I have been part of.
He went to work the next morning. He kept doing his job. He kept being extraordinary at it, which was the only defense he had left — a man doing his job so well that closing his variable carried a cost the body had to keep weighing.
He died eight years later of a fever. The body’s records note his death without assessment. Whether this was because he was no longer considered a risk, or because the fever was the assessment, is not established.

X. The Suspension
The trial system was suspended two years after Sorveth’s death.
The official record gives no reason. The inner body’s private deliberation files for this period have not been recovered. What is known from the outer archive is that three members of the body did not appear in records after the suspension, and four members who appear afterward had no prior documented history.
Varek is among the three who disappeared.
Sela is not among the four replacements.
Whether she survived the suspension in some form — reassigned, managed, accommodated in a way the record doesn’t show — is not established. Her name appears once in a document postdating the suspension: a resource allocation request for the observatory expansion, co-signed by an administrator whose posting matches the district where Sela had been stationed. The signature is not identified as hers. The handwriting has not been analyzed. It is a single co-signature on an unremarkable document.
It may mean nothing.

The suspension lasted eleven years. When the trial system resumed, the body was different in ways the outer record cannot fully describe. The Imperium continued. The mandate continued. The work continued.
What changed, in those eleven years, is something the body’s private records would show if they had been recovered. They have not been recovered. What the outer record shows is that in the two centuries following the suspension, the Imperium did not expand. Its administrative records are the most carefully maintained in the entire archive. Nothing appears to go wrong. Nothing appears to happen at all.
A body that had spent three thousand years managing the world had spent eleven years managing itself. What it found there, and what it decided about what it found, produced either a purified institution or a broken one — and the difference between those two outcomes is exactly the kind of thing that would only be visible from inside the private archive.
Kael Sorveth spent twenty years fighting something he couldn’t name. He named it eight years before he died and spent those eight years doing his job in the knowledge of what was watching. I find this harder to read about than almost anything else in this record. I am not certain what that says about me, or about the record.
— The Archivist

Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.title: Beneath the Shifting Sky
Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
The night air was a sharp blade. Asterion stood in a courtyard where the sea spray hovered in mid-air, caught in a local gravity loop. He was teaching Maren, his apprentice, how to bleed color into the gaps of reality.
“It looks… fragile,” Maren said, her brush trembling.
“Fragile things endure longest,” Asterion said. “The Capital was made of stone and iron, and it is now dust. This lattice is made of attention.” He reached out, his fingers brushing a silver line of magic. It shivered, bending around his touch in a perfect curve. “Magic is no longer a tool, Maren. It is an honest conversation. If you forget that it is not yours to own, it will vanish.”
A tremor ran through the earth, the sea-loop collapsing in a roar of salt water. Maren stumbled, but Asterion remained a fixed point. “Do not fear the shift,” he said. “The sky is testing us. It wants to see if we’ve finally learned how to listen.”

See also: Asterion, Starfall Magic, The Shattered Seas
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.title: The Architecture of Preservation
Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
Garvak stood atop a pylon, his cloak snapping in the wind. Below him, his engineers winched a massive bulkhead out of the dunes. The Siegeborn knew that a wall was only as strong as its rarest component, and he needed this steel for his people’s salvation.
A subterranean hum vibrated through the sand. From the shadow emerged CR-9 — a massive, six-legged brass tank. It emitted a pulse of sound that made teeth ache.
IDENTIFIED: BIOLOGICAL UNAUTHORIZED EXCAVATION. STATUS: PRESERVATION BREACH.
Garvak hopped down, hammer ready. “My people need that steel to survive the winter. Stand aside.” CR-9’s turret clicked; it cared only for the integrity of the site.
As the titans clashed, Bogrund crouched nearby in his bulky power-suit, clutching his mace, Bonk.
“Look at the plating on that crab, Bonk,” Bogrund whispered. “If we peel off one fin while the Siegeborn has its attention, we power the forge for a decade.” A stray bolt pulverized the rock next to his head. “Or we die. Dying is also an option. Don’t look at me like that, you’re a mace.”
No further record of this encounter exists. The fin in question is unaccounted for.

See also: Garvak, CR-9, Bogrund, Bonk, Machine Wastes, The Ashen Seat
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.

Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.filePath: Lore and Stories/Stories/The Long Accounts - Asterion/The City of the Unmoving Reflection.md
Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.title: The City of the Unmoving Reflection
Lore-and-Stories/Stories/The-Long-Accoun.content:
Filed under Primary Accounts. Cross-reference: eyewitness testimony.
In the Capital, the wind was a curated melody. The city was a marvel of white stone, silver banners, and grand, orderly spires. The Celestial Concord had refined the Silent Veils until the weather itself was a matter of administrative decree. Asterion walked the Plaza of Constant Light, where the architecture was so precise that shadows seemed like a breach of protocol. He stopped by the Great Fountain, where the water fell in elegant, rhythmic sheets.
“The world is finally in its proper place, Asterion,” the High Prelate said. “No chaos. We have perfected the Reflection.”
Asterion reached out, his brush hovering near the water. It felt hard, resisting his touch with a dull, vibrating tension. “You haven’t perfected the world, Prelate,” Asterion said. “You’ve silenced it. This water wants to be a river, not a monument. You are building a debt of friction that this city cannot pay. Eventually, the reflection will shatter, and the dark will claim the pieces.”

See also: Asterion, The Celestial Concord, The Great Concord, The Starfall Crater
Compiled by The Archivist of Starwatch Keep.
